activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other.
story:
The travel agency smelled of brochures and the coconut hand cream Mr. Visser rubbed into his knuckles every afternoon, and Antoine had memorized the wall of destinations without ever having been further from home than a school trip to the provincial capital. He shelved pamphlets for river cruises he could not afford, and between customers he kept his laptop open behind the till, a city map glowing under his hands. In the evenings he was taking a course in geographic information systems, because Mr. Visser had said, the day Antoine was hired, that a boy who wanted to see the world ought first to learn how to read it.

The project was due Friday: overlay a flood risk layer on a housing map and write what the picture argued. Antoine had chosen the city where his grandmother had lived, a river town he half-remembered, and at first the assignment had seemed almost too easy. Then he opened the flood layer and the river ran straight through the middle of city hall, through the courthouse, through a park that sat on a hill no water could ever reach.

He leaned closer. Behind him the door chimed and Yara came in, school bag over one shoulder, and dropped into the chair meant for honeymoon planners. "Tell me you finished."

"Look at this." He turned the screen toward her. The river crossed the buildings like a joke drawn on in pen.

Yara squinted. "Is that wrong, or is that real? Didn't your cousin say the whole downtown floods?"

"Not through city hall. My grandmother used to sit on those steps." He thought of the summer he was eleven, the river two streets over and brown and swollen, his grandmother watching it from her kitchen window while she told him the flood of her childhood had taken the houses on Dreef Street and spared the brick ones, that the water was capricious and chose its favourites. He had believed her completely then. He wanted the map to tell him whether she had been telling the truth.

He checked the housing layer alone. Buildings sat where buildings should sit. He checked the flood layer alone. The river curved where he remembered it curving. Only together did they lie.

"Maybe the maps are from different years," Yara said.

"Both current." He scrolled through the software's menus, past tools whose names he only half knew, and found, buried in the layer properties, a field labelled with a string of letters and numbers, different for each file. The flood layer said one thing. The housing layer said another.

Waylon arrived to buy a rail pass he could have bought online, and stood over them with his elbows on the counter. "That's ugly," he said of the river through city hall.

"It's not ugly, it's wrong." Antoine kept reading. The course notes were on his phone, and in week three, a line he had skimmed and forgotten now surfaced plain: GIS layers stored in different coordinate reference systems will not line up correctly until one is reprojected to match the other. He said it out loud, slowly, the way his grandmother used to read back a phone number.

"So fix it," Waylon said.

Antoine found the reprojection tool. He chose the flood layer, chose the housing layer's reference system as the target, and ran it. The screen thought for a moment. The river slid sideways, half a neighbourhood's width, and settled into its banks. City hall stood dry on its hill. The water now lapped at exactly the streets his grandmother had named, Dreef and the two roads behind it, and at a stretch of new flats Antoine recognized from his cousin's photos, buildings with balconies and a playground, all of it coloured red on the risk layer.

Nobody spoke. The door chimed behind them and Mr. Visser came out from the back, drying his hands, and looked at the screen over the counter.

"That's the flood map," Antoine said. "Those new apartments are inside it."

Mr. Visser put on his reading glasses. He had sold holidays in that city for thirty years and knew its hotel names the way Antoine knew bus routes. He was quiet for a long moment, and Antoine braced for the older man to excoriate the mapmakers, or the developers, or the municipal office that had zoned the land, but Mr. Visser only said, "The Mercurius. I've put four couples there this spring."

"They're in the red zone," Antoine said.

"According to that." Mr. Visser tapped the housing layer with one finger, careful of the screen. "You trust both maps?"

Antoine looked at the river sitting obediently between its banks. He trusted the alignment now, that was mechanical, provable, a thing the software either did or did not do. But the flood layer itself came from a model, and models had authors, and he did not know who had drawn the boundary or how old the rainfall data was or whether the new flats had been raised on fill that changed the answer. "I trust that they line up," he said. "The rest I'd have to check."

Yara wrote down the street names anyway. Her aunt rented in one of the red buildings, and she took a photo of the screen with the park and the river and the playground all in frame.

Friday he submitted the overlay with a paragraph on what remained uncertain, and by Saturday Mr. Visser had asked him to print the map, which now hung taped to the agency window between the cruises and the islands, facing the street. A woman stopped outside it for a long time that afternoon, one hand on a stroller, then came in and asked which streets, exactly, the red reached.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
The piano had stood in his grandfather's front room for eleven summers, and Alexis had never once touched it. He touched it now, because the summer before college had emptied itself of everything else, and because his grandfather had said, one evening over dinner, "You could learn. I won't be around to teach you twice." So Alexis came every Tuesday and Friday, took the bus out past the ring road, and practiced scales on an instrument that smelled of dust and lemon polish and, faintly, of the cigarettes his grandfather had given up in 1998.

The first thing he did, waiting for his grandfather to finish his coffee, was count the keys. He started with the white ones, running a finger along them like a man counting fence posts. Fifty-two. Then the black ones, which went faster because they were thinner, grouped in twos and threes like people waiting for a bus. Thirty-six. He added it in his head, then checked it on his phone. Eighty-eight. He texted Loan, who replied, "cool. adrian says his keyboard has 61. you win." It was a small victory, but Alexis held it all the way through dinner.

His grandfather taught him the way old men teach, which is to say obdurately. Wrists level. Fingers curled. Again. The C major scale, then the same scale with the left hand an octave down, then both hands together, which was like patting your head and rubbing your stomach while someone vilified your ancestry from across the room. His grandfather did not vilify, exactly. He only said "again," and Alexis discovered that a single word, repeated with enough patience, could do the work of a whole lecture.

"You're counting," his grandfather said one Friday in July, listening to Alexis stumble through a simple Bach minuet.

"I'm not."

"You pause where the page is clean. You rush where there are lots of notes. You are playing arithmetic, not music." He set down his coffee. "The eighty-eight are all there ever were. Fifty-two white, thirty-six black. Stop checking whether you've covered them. They'll still be there."

From the doorway, unseen, the old man watched his grandson argue back, and it pleased him more than he showed. The boy said something about efficiency, about optimising practice, about how he had read online that deliberate practice meant identifying errors and targeting them. The words came out of him like the college brochure they surely had. And yet his hands, when he returned to the minuet, did something his mouth had not authorised. They slowed down. They lingered on the third bar, where the melody dipped into a minor key for two beats, a small darkness that the boy played again, and then again, without counting anything.

Alexis noticed it himself a week later, on a Tuesday when the room was hot and the window stood open onto the neighbour's garden, where Mr. Girma was watering his tomatoes and singing something in a language Alexis didn't recognise. The minuet had stopped being a task. The two-beat dip had become the reason he played the rest of it. He thought of Loan, who practiced free throws by shooting a hundred a day, and of Adrian, who refused to practice at all and said repetition killed spontaneity, and he thought, for the first time, that both of them were half right in a way that made each whole. The scales and the lingering were not opposites. They lived together, the way Mr. Girma's tomatoes and his singing did, some symbiosis Alexis could name but not yet explain, discipline feeding the thing it seemed to constrain.

"I want to learn a piece," he told his grandfather in August. "A real one. Not a minuet from a book for children."

"Which piece?"

Alexis had one ready, a Chopin nocturne he'd heard in a film, and he played the opening eight bars from memory, badly, with the pedal down too long so the notes blurred into each other like wet ink. His grandfather said nothing. He got up, went to the sideboard, and took out a photograph Alexis had never seen: his grandmother, young, standing beside this same piano in a different house, hands resting on the closed lid.

"She was the player," his grandfather said. "Not me. I tuned it. Fifty-three years I tuned it and never learned a note." He set the photograph on the music stand, where the sheet music should have been. "You counted the keys the first day you came. Eighty-eight. I watched you do it."

Alexius felt his face go warm. "I thought you were making coffee."

"I was. Then I watched." His grandfather sat back down. "It's not a crime, counting. But she never counted. She sat down and the eighty-eight were hers." He tapped the photograph. "Fifty-two white, thirty-six black, and not one of them ever knew it was being counted."

The nocturne was, his grandfather admitted, probably two years beyond him. Alexis decided to start it anyway. He set the photograph on the sideboard, facing the bench, and opened the book to the first page, where the printed notes ran up and down like a fence he had once counted post by post. Mr. Girma's singing drifted through the window. Alexis put his hands on the keys, and the first chord came out blurred, wrong, beautiful.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Sea ice reflects most sunlight while open ocean absorbs most of it, so melting ice exposes darker water that warms and melts more ice: a reinforcing feedback loop.
story:
The community garden had three days of water left in the rain barrels, and the city's hose permit expired at the end of the month, which meant Vanessa had until Saturday to convince the other plot holders that tearing up half the beds for a rain-catching system was worth it. She had the numbers in her notebook: last summer's rainfall, the barrel capacity, the square footage of the shed roof. She also had Joe, who thought the whole thing was a waste of a perfectly good Saturday, and Teagan, who agreed with Vanessa in principle but hated arguing in front of the whole garden.

The argument was scheduled for the Thursday meeting, so Vanessa spent Tuesday evening at the garden after Ms. Fraser's science class, pulling bindweed and rehearsing. In class that morning Ms. Fraser had drawn a circle on the whiteboard, sunlight bouncing off a pale surface, then drawn the same sunlight sinking into a dark one, and asked the room what happened when the pale surface shrank. Nobody answered fast enough, so she had said it herself: sea ice reflects most sunlight while open ocean absorbs most of it, so melting ice exposes darker water that warms and melts more ice. Then she had written "reinforcing feedback loop" on the board and told them the Arctic was running one in real time.

Vanessa turned that over while she worked. The garden was its own small system. Cheap water from the city permit meant nobody had bothered with the roof; when the permit prices went up, which the newsletter said they would, half the plot holders would quit because they were on fixed incomes and the wealthy ones would just pay. She could see the loop: less participation, less lobbying for the permit subsidy, higher prices, less participation. The dark water spreading.

"You're staring at the compost again," Teagan said, arriving with her bicycle helmet still on. Teagan's father worked at the plant nursery that donated seedlings every spring, which was why Teagan never had to argue about anything; the garden needed her family more than the other way around.

"I'm thinking about ice," Vanessa said. "Ms. Fraser's thing. Ice reflects sunlight, ocean absorbs it, so when the ice melts the water warms and melts more ice. It feeds itself." She wiped her hands on her shorts. "The garden does the same thing. Not sunlight. Money."

Teagan sat on the edge of the barrel platform. "That's a stretch."

"Is it? If we lose the low-income permit, we lose Mrs. Okafor and the Alvarez family and the guys from the halfway house. Then it's just people who can afford anything, and they don't need the subsidy, so the city cuts it, and then more people leave."

The Thursday meeting was held on folding chairs between the bean trellises. The garden coordinator read the agenda, and when the rain system came up, Joe stood up first. He was seventeen and worked weekends at the hardware store, and he talked like a salesman because he was one. "We have water now," he said. "The permit's thirty dollars. The gutters and tanks you're talking about are six hundred. That's not activism, that's arithmetic."

Vanessa had expected this. What she hadn't expected was the nodding, the murmur of agreement, the way the whole semicircle of chairs leaned slightly toward Joe the way plants lean toward a window. A foreboding settled in her stomach, not dramatic, just the plain recognition that she was about to lose. She stood up anyway.

"Joe's right about the arithmetic," she said, and watched him blink. "Thirty dollars this year. The newsletter says the subsidized rate ends in January because participation dropped below the threshold the parks department uses. So next year it's a hundred and ten, and every year after that more, because when people quit, the subsidy looks even less justified." She held up her notebook, though nobody could read it from the chairs. "It's like the ice thing. Ice reflects most sunlight and open ocean absorbs most of it, so melting ice exposes darker water that warms and melts more ice. The melt feeds the melt. Our costs feed our costs. Joe's arithmetic is one year of a loop."

Ms. Fraser, who kept a pepper plot two rows over and had said nothing all evening, raised her hand as if she were still in her own classroom. "I can verify the permit notice," she said. "It's on the city website. She's not inventing it."

The vote was eleven to nine, with Joe abstaining. The rain barrels would go up on the shed before the first September storm, funded by a plant sale Teagan's father agreed to supply at cost, which Teagan negotiated on the spot in a low voice while the coordinator was still counting hands. Vanessa felt the win and also the shape of what she couldn't know: whether the subsidy would actually survive, whether the storm would actually come, whether the weather, which had been capricious all summer, would fill the tanks or pass them by. She had spent two weeks proselytizing about rainfall to anyone who would stand still, and she still could not promise rain.

Afterward, Joe helped her carry the folding chairs to the shed. "You could have just said it was expensive next year," he said. "You didn't need the polar bear stuff."

"Maybe not," Vanessa said. She stacked the last chair and latched the door. "But you didn't argue with the loop."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Supercompensation is the idea that the body gets fitter during recovery after training, when it rebuilds beyond its previous level, not during the workout itself.
story:
Alex arrived at the rink before six again, his skates already soft at the ankles from a season of daily use. He had not missed a morning in five weeks, and he was getting slower. His lap times, which he kept in a spiral notebook in his bag, had drifted up by almost a second and a half, and his legs felt like wet rope by the second set of drills. He told himself it was the cold, then the ice, then a growth spurt, but none of those explanations survived contact with the notebook, which was obdurate in the way only numbers written in your own handwriting can be.

Finley found him on the bench after the public skate, lacing up for what would have been his second session of the day. "You look like a guy who lost an argument with a Zamboni," she said, dropping onto the boards beside him.

"I'm getting slower and I'm training more than anyone here." He flipped the notebook open to the page of lap times and turned it toward her. "Every day. Two sessions half the time. Explain that."

Finley studied the columns the way she studied a chemistry problem, chewing the cap of her pen. "Mr. Robinson had a chart about this in his office. Something about recovery. I took a photo of it because I thought it was funny." She scrolled through her phone, then held it out. The chart showed fitness rising after a workout, dipping first, then climbing above where it had started.

"That's the part nobody believes," she said. "The dip. You're weaker right after you train, and then the body rebuilds past where it was. But only if you let it. It's called supercompensation." She tapped the rising line. "The fitter happens after. Not during."

Alex stared at the little graph and felt something rearrange itself, the way a room looks different once you move one chair. "So I've been starting every session before the rebuild finishes."

"Basically you've been sawing the board shorter every day and measuring it twice as much."

Lyam skated over before Alex could answer, spraying a deliberate arc of ice against the boards. "Morning grind, brother. Day forty, right? You're a machine." Lyam was the kind of teammate the younger kids lionize, all hustle and no notebook, and Alex had spent five weeks trying to become him. Now the effort looked different, like he'd been copying a homework style instead of learning the subject.

"Actually," Alex said, and paused, because the next part embarrassed him. "I'm taking tomorrow off. And Wednesday. I'm making a schedule. Warm-ups, hard days, rest days. Finley's helping."

Lyam's face did something complicated. "Rest days are for guys who don't want it."

"I want it," Alex said. "That's kind of the whole point. I want it and I'm slower than I was in October." He heard his own voice go flat and earnest and decided not to fix it. Around them the rink emptied, the last few skaters drifting toward the exits, the overhead lights buzzing down to half.

They stayed while the Zamboni made its slow luminous passes, and Alex sketched the week in the notebook, his hand unsure. Two hard days, then a rest day, then a lighter one, a warm-up block before everything, the structure foreign on the page the way a new language is foreign, correct but not yet his. "I don't know if this is right," he admitted to Finley. "I'm guessing at the spacing. There's no way to know except trying it and finding out."

"That's how anyone knows anything," Finley said. "My philosophy teacher calls it epistemology. It sounds fancier than 'try it and see,' but it's the same shape."

"Everything about my body, I got from someone telling me. Push harder. No days off. Nobody ever showed me a chart going down before it goes up." He closed the notebook and slid it into his bag, the strap worn pale where it crossed his chest every morning. On the ice the Zamboni finished its last pass and the surface lay blank and perfect, unmarked by a single track.

Lyam watched it too, and for a moment the performance dropped out of his shoulders. "How will you know if it's working?"

"The notebook," Alex said, standing, hoisting the bag. "Same as before. The difference is now I'll know what I'm actually measuring."

He walked out through the pro shop, past the stick rack and the freezer of pucks, and pushed the heavy door open into the cold parking lot, where his breath hung in the streetlight. Tomorrow morning, for the first time in forty days, he would not be here, and the thought felt like falling and like standing still at once. He put his key in the car door and stopped, looking back at the rink's grey flank, at the one window still glowing above the ice.

"Day one," he said to nobody, and got in.

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: Accounting profit subtracts only money actually paid out, while economic profit also subtracts implicit costs such as the owner's time and the next-best use of their money.
story:
Cameron had worked Saturdays at Khan's Hardware for eleven months, which was long enough to know which keys stuck on the register and which regulars paid in coins counted out one at a time. It was a slow afternoon in June, the kind when the ceiling fan moved the heat around rather than removing it, and he was restocking washers when Adrianna came through the door holding her phone like evidence.

"Look," she said, turning the screen toward him. It was a spreadsheet, tidy and colour-coded, sales on top, costs below, a green number at the bottom. "Four hundred dollars this month. From my shop. That's real money, Cameron. I told my dad I'm done applying to the tutoring place."

He set down the box of washers. He had seen the number before, or one like it, in his own head. Last autumn, before the hardware store, he had spent every Saturday restoring a bicycle he planned to resell, telling himself the parts only cost him thirty dollars. When he finally sold it for ninety, he had felt rich for exactly one evening, until he did the arithmetic again in bed. Six Saturdays. He had paid himself nothing for any of them. The thirty-dollar parts and the sixty-dollar difference were what an accountant would call his profit, but the Saturdays were gone, and Saturdays, it turned out, had a price. That was the month he'd taken the job at Ms. Khan's, where Saturdays were worth nine dollars an hour and he could stop pretending they were free.

"Your costs," he said to Adrianna. "What's in that column?"

"Fabric, shipping, the listing fees. I keep every receipt."

"Hours?"

She frowned at him. "My hours are free. It's my own time."

Behind the counter, Ms. Khan was pricing paintbrushes and not looking up, though Cameron could tell she was listening, the way she always listened while pretending to inventory. He pulled a receipt pad toward him and wrote Adrianna's green number at the top. "How many hours a week?"

"I don't know. Maybe fifteen. Photographing stuff, sewing, answering messages at midnight."

He did the multiplication and wrote it under the sales, then subtracted. The number at the bottom came out negative, and he watched her face as she read it, the small collapse of the green figure into something sullen and smaller than a loss. She took the pen from him and crossed out his line, then uncrossed it, then sat down on a stack of fertilizer bags as though the floor had shifted to destabilize her.

"That's not how business works," she said. "Nobody counts it like that."

"The money one does," Cameron said. "Accounting profit subtracts only what you actually paid out." He tapped his line. "Economic profit subtracts your hours too. And what the money would've made somewhere else. My dad calls it the next-best thing you gave up."

Ms. Khan set down her pricing gun. "He calls it a maxim, does he?"

"He calls it a headache," Cameron said, and Adrianna laughed despite herself, which felt like the first honest thing either of them had done in five minutes.

She stayed while he rang up a woman buying a hacksaw and a length of chain, and while he swept, she kept working the receipt pad, splitting her hours into the ones she loved, the midnight sewing, and the ones she only tolerated, the shipping and the photography. "What if I paid someone for the parts I hate," she said, not quite asking him. "Tate would do the photos for almost nothing. Then my hours are only the ones I'd spend anyway." She redrew the columns. The number was still negative, but it was less negative, and she stared at it the way people stare at a door that has opened a crack.

"You could still take the tutoring job," Cameron said. "Do the shop smaller. Only the things that sell." He didn't say the rest, which was that he had made the opposite choice, trading the bicycle work for the register, and that some Saturdays he still felt the subtraction.

Ms. Khan locked the till at six and handed him his envelope, cash as always, the wage he had stopped thinking of as free. Outside, the heat had softened, and Adrianna was sitting on the curb with the phone at her ear, saying, "Tate, how do you feel about lighting?"

Cameron pushed his earnings deep into his pocket and started toward the bus stop, hearing her say, before the door swung shut behind him, "No, describe it to me like I'm buying it."

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In his 1961 book Griff nach der Weltmacht, German historian Fritz Fischer argued that Imperial Germany deliberately pursued a world war, setting off a long debate known as the Fischer controversy.
story:
The monument stood where the road bent, a granite obelisk with forty-one names cut into its base, and Ryan had walked past it for eleven years without reading any of them. Now he stood in front of it with two textbooks in his backpack and a Monday deadline, and read the first name twice because the light was going and the letters were shallow. Shiloh crouched at the far panel with her phone, taking pictures of the section where the stone was a slightly different colour, newer, as if the town had remembered someone late.

"The chapter's useless," Jalen said, dropping onto the monument's bottom step. He had the school's older textbook open on his knee, spine cracked, margins full of some previous student's pencil. "Mine says the war came about through alliances and mobilization timetables, basically nobody's fault, everyone sleepwalking in. What does yours say?"

Ryan read the relevant paragraph aloud, the cold making his voice flat. His book, the new edition, put it differently: German leaders had sought a large war, had gambled on it. "Ours makes it sound like Germany wanted it. Yours makes it sound like a machine nobody was driving." The two sentences sat side by side in his head and refused to merge.

"That can't both be true," Shiloh said, not looking up from her photographing. "Unless." She stopped there, the way she did when an idea was still soft, and waved him over instead. The newer panel held six names, added decades after the first thirty-five, and one of them had been recut, the letters deeper than the others, a repair. "Look at this. Somebody put these names on after. Whatever record they used, it was wrong once, or incomplete, and somebody else fixed it later."

Behind them a car door closed, and Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya came up the path with a bag of cleaning cloths, the retired teacher who apparently had keys to every public stone in the county. He began wiping lichen from the base without greeting them, which was his form of greeting. Ryan, who had spent a semester being cautiously polite to him and refusing to be a sycophant about it, asked anyway, because the deadline was real: why would two textbooks disagree about something that happened over a hundred years ago?

"Come Sunday I'll be cleaning this thing again," Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya said, wringing the cloth. "Ask me then."

Jalen groaned. Shiloh laughed. But Ryan found he couldn't let it go, and later that night, at the kitchen table with both books open and the monument photographs on his screen, he searched the old textbook's citation trail, then the new one's, following footnotes the way you follow a voice in another room. Both books leaned on German historians. The older one on a generation who wrote in the ruins of a different war, careful men who wanted, he thought, to sublimate a national guilt into something systemic, structures instead of intentions. The newer one cited a single work at the root of everything: a 1961 book called Griff nach der Weltmacht, by a German historian named Fritz Fischer, who had argued that Imperial Germany had deliberately pursued a world war.

He sat with that for a long moment. Then he searched further and found the argument had not settled anything; it had set off a running battle among historians that had a name. On Sunday he brought both books to the monument, where Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya was already working, and said, "It's called the Fischer controversy, isn't it." Not quite a question.

"Very good," the old man said, without pausing. "Sixty years they've been at it. Historians disagree, young man, because their sources are partial and their questions keep changing. The answers change because the questions do." Ryan noticed that the man had, after all, said something like a speech, and that it sounded less like wisdom than like tiredness. He looked down at the recut name on the newer panel, the one that had been wrong once and corrected, and understood that he could write his essay neither as the old book nor the new one, but as the gap between them, the controversy itself, and still not know which side was right, only that each side had asked a different question of the same broken record.

Shiloh arrived with coffee for three, epicurean about it, insisting on the good place across from the library rather than the gas station, and handed Ryan his cup. "So what's the answer?" she said. Ryan looked at the forty-one names, at the stone that had been corrected once and might need correcting again, and said, "Ask me in fifty years."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Binary search needs to jump straight to the middle item, so it loses its advantage on a linked list, where reaching the middle means walking through the items one by one.
story:
The basement smelled like dryer sheets and old carpet, and Kaitlyn's laptop sat on a folding table between two milk crates of her mother's canning jars. Noah pulled his chair closer and opened his notebook to the page where he'd copied the algorithm in blue pen, though the pen had run dry halfway through the last line and the rest faded to a scratch.

"You're sure this is worth it?" Kaitlyn asked. She had a stats test on Monday and had brought her flashcards down anyway, as if to propitiate some god of productivity while she watched him work. "Two hours of my basement for a phone app that tells you if a word is on a banned list."

"It's not banned," Noah said. "It's a word list for the spell check thing Estelle wants for the literary magazine. Sixty thousand words, alphabetical. She asked if searching it could be faster."

"And can it?"

"That's what I'm building." He turned the laptop toward her. The words were loaded into a structure he'd made in second period, each entry pointing to the next, like a train of boxcars. He'd been proud of it at the time, proud enough to show Ms. Hernández after class, and she had looked at it for a long moment, reticent in the way she got when a student's work was correct and beside the point at the same time. "Nice linked list," was all she'd said. He hadn't understood the pause until now, and maybe he still didn't.

He typed the new function the way the notebook described: find the middle, compare, throw away half, repeat. Binary search, the handout called it, and the handout had promised something dramatic, log time, the kind of phrase that sounded like a spell. Kaitlyn shuffled her flashcards and watched the screen over his shoulder, which he liked, even if he would never have said so.

Last summer, before any of this, he'd spent an entire afternoon looking for a single document on his father's filing shelf, checking folder after folder from the top down, and his father had come in, gone straight to the middle of the shelf, looked at the label, and moved one section to the left. "The shelf's alphabetical," his father had said. "Stop being a machine and start being a person." Noah had thought about that for months without knowing it was a lesson he'd be tested on.

The code ran. He pulled up his test harness, the one that timed a hundred thousand lookups, and pressed enter. The number came back and sat there on the screen. He looked at it, then looked at the old number in his notes, the one from the linear version, where the program started at the first word and walked forward until it found what it wanted. They were the same. Not close. The same.

"That's broken," Kaitlyn said.

"It's not broken." He ran it again. Same number, give or take a few milliseconds, like the machine shrugging. He sat back and put both hands in his hair. Somewhere upstairs her mother ran water for dishes, and a jar of tomatoes from 2019 caught the light of the utility bulb like something being kept safe.

He started tracing it by hand, on paper, where things made sense. Find the middle, the algorithm said, so he went to find the middle. To get to the middle of his word list, he had to start at the first entry and follow the pointers forward, one, then one, then one, thirty thousand times, because there was no shelf to put his hand on, no way to jump. His father had gone straight to the middle of the alphabet. His program had to walk there. And after it walked there and compared and threw away half the list, it had to walk again to the middle of whichever half remained.

"It's the search that's smart," he said slowly, "and the storage that's stupid. I taught it the smart part and kept the dumb part."

"Can you fix the dumb part?"

"Maybe. I'd have to store the words differently, in something where you can jump. I haven't learned that yet." He closed the notebook. The faded last line bothered him now, like a sentence he'd only half finished saying.

Kaitlyn set her flashcards down. "So it's not faster at all. Exactly the same speed."

"For this," Noah said. "On this. That's the part the handout didn't say." He was quiet for a second, because there was a larger honest thing underneath and he wasn't sure he could lift it yet: that he didn't know whether the answer was a better structure or a different way of thinking about the one he had, whether Ms. Hernández had seen this exact failure coming in his boxcars, whether his father's shelf was a lesson about data or just a tired man finding a paper. All of that stayed open, and he let it stay open.

He texted Estelle anyway: found the trick, also found the trap, will explain tomorrow, bring snacks as recompense for making you wait. Then he opened a new file, titled it the way his father had said it, and started typing.

"Stop being a machine," Kaitlyn read off the screen.

"Start being a person," Noah said, and hit run.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Ontario high school students must complete 40 hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma.
story:
Nevaeh had been told the food bank shared a building with the animal shelter, but nobody had warned her about the smell, which arrived before she even reached the door: kibble and bleach and something funkier underneath, like a wet coat left in a locker since September. Inside, the front half held cages, and behind a partition marked COMMUNITY FOOD PROGRAM was a long room with folding tables, cardboard boxes, and a woman in a lanyard directing two girls Nevaeh recognized from school. The woman turned out to be Ms. Cheung, who ran both operations, apparently on the theory that hungry people and homeless animals were a staffing problem she could solve with the same volunteers.

"You must be Nevaeh," Ms. Cheung said, handing her a clipboard before she'd finished saying hello. "Signed waiver?"

"Here. And I have to log hours today, if that matters."

"It matters to you, I assume, or you'd be home." Ms. Cheung's tone was incisive but not unkind, the voice of someone who had processed four hundred clipboards and did not require small talk. "Stacey will show you the sorting table."

Stacey, it emerged, was the taller of the two girls, and she had opinions. She explained the expiry-date system, the dented-can protocol, and the correct way to stack pasta so the boxes didn't avalanche, all in the manner of a person who had been here since September and considered the sorting table a personal fiefdom. The other girl, Miranda, mostly labeled bags and offered commentary.

"She's here for the diploma," Miranda said, nodding at Nevaeh. "Aren't you in grade twelve? Everyone in grade twelve shows up in spring like locusts."

"I'm not a locust," Nevaeh said. "I'm a person with a deadline."

"We all did it," Stacey said, with a shrug that excoriated both of them and also, somehow, herself. "Ontario high school students have to complete forty hours of community involvement to earn the Ontario Secondary School Diploma. Forty. Which is why in June this place is full of people who spent eleven months not caring."

Nevaeh slid a can of chickpeas into a crate and considered whether to be insulted. It was true she had put this off. It was also true that she'd spent the morning before coming here arguing with her mother about whether community hours were a punishment or a privilege, her mother holding the first position on the grounds that mandatory kindness was an oxymoron, and Nevaeh unable to articulate why that felt wrong. Stacey had just handed her the vocabulary, though Nevaeh doubted Stacey knew it.

"Is that why you're here?" Nevaeh asked. "The forty?"

"I finished mine last year." Stacey taped a box shut with more force than the box required. "I stayed because of the dogs."

Miranda snorted. "She's on a sabbatical from the cats. One of them took a piece out of her wrist in October."

"He was misunderstood."

This was the point at which the morning became actual work. A delivery arrived, forty boxes of donated goods from a grocery chain's expired-line shelf, and for two hours Nevaeh sorted cereal from soap, discovered that people donate a truly astonishing quantity of expired cake mix, and learned that a jar with no lid is not a donation but a biohazard according to Stacey, who had apparently lobbied Ms. Cheung to have this written into official policy. At one point a volunteer from the shelter side came through carrying a basset hound who had eaten an entire bag of donated rice, and the whole room stopped to watch them go, the dog wearing the serene expression of a creature with no regrets and no diploma requirements.

At the lunch break, Nevaeh sat on the loading dock with her log sheet and a pen. Thirty-four hours already recorded from tutoring at the library, six left. Six hours, one Saturday, and the OSSD was hers. She could write down today's four, come back once more, and be finished, and she would have done it, and it would mean exactly what the province said it meant, which was nothing anyone could measure.

"I take it back," she said, when Stacey came out with a sandwich. "About the deadline. I mean, I still have it. But my mom said this was forced labour, and I was going to be cynical about it, and now I can't decide."

"You can't decide what?"

"Whether it counts if you're made to do it. Or whether it only counts if you'd come anyway." Nevaeh looked at the log sheet, then at the door where the basset hound had been carried off to whatever restorative justice awaited him. "You came anyway. But you started because of the hours."

"Started because my mom signed me up," Stacey said. "Same thing, worse."

"That's not an answer."

"It's not," Stacey agreed, unwrapping her sandwich. "Miranda started because of the hours and she's still here and she complains every single day. I complain less. You'll figure out which one you are by about August."

Inside, a dog began to howl, joined by a second, and Ms. Cheung's voice carried over both, calling for someone to take the next pallet of rice.

"Coming," Nevaeh called back, and went.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The GED tests were created in 1942 to let military service members and veterans who had not finished high school show high-school-level skills.
story:
The folding chairs had been set in crooked rows on the football field, and Katherine, sixteen and graduating a full two years before anyone had expected her to, sat in the front row pretending the sun wasn't melting her. In her speech, folded into a square in her blazer pocket, she had written a paragraph about her grandfather, who she had always believed had finished high school in this same town, class of some far-off year, and had kept a varnished diploma on the workroom wall. She had written that he had walked across a stage like this one. She was third in the line of speakers, which meant she had eleven minutes to decide whether any of it was true.

Beside her, Keanna leaned over and pinched the hem of Katherine's gown. "You're going to pass out," Keanna said. "Your knee is doing the thing."

"My knee is quiescent," Katherine said. "It has been instructed to remain so."

"Your knee did not get that instruction."

Behind them, Crystal was taking photographs of everyone's shoes. Katherine's grandmother sat three rows back in the visitor section, holding her program like a hymnal, wearing the good coat even in the heat because some occasions, in her accounting, demanded it.

The principal said the usual things. Katherine half listened and half rehearsed, and it occurred to her, with the particular dread of a person who has just checked a locked door twice, that she had never actually seen the diploma on the workroom wall. She had seen a frame. She had seen, at seven years old, something official-looking, and she had built a man on top of it. She turned around to find her grandmother, who was already looking at her, and her grandmother gave a small wave that Katherine returned too slowly.

When the graduates were called to file toward the stage, she detoured past the visitor section, claiming a shoelace, a sip of water, a reason. She crouched beside her grandmother's chair. "Did Pop finish high school? Here?"

Her grandmother looked at her for a long moment. "You put that in your speech."

"It's in my speech."

"He never finished school. He left to serve." Her grandmother smoothed the program on her knee. "The army gave him a way, though. They made the GED tests in 1942, for servicemen and veterans who hadn't finished high school, so they could show they had the skills. He took it after he came home."

Katherine's face went hot in a way that had nothing to do with the sun. "So he didn't walk across a stage."

"He walked across a different one," her grandmother said. "At a base, with his dress shoes. He was prouder of that than of anything else he ever did, and he'd have skinned you for pretending it was the other kind." Then, softer, because she was a woman who noticed when a girl was about to come apart over a folded square of paper: "Change it. You have time. And then come sit by me after, and I'll tell you the part about the dress shoes."

The line was moving. Keanna, four chairs ahead, was gesturing at her with increasing urgency, and Crystal had abandoned the shoes entirely and was filming Katherine's walk toward the stage as though it were a hostage negotiation. Ms. Johansson, marshaling the graduates at the steps, took Katherine's elbow without a word and said, "Breathe. Then fix it. You've got until they finish the science awards."

Katherine stood at the edge of the stage and unfolded her speech against her knee. The paragraph about her grandfather was two hundred words of a story she had wanted to be true because it made her early graduation seem like an inheritance rather than an accident. She had told it so often, to Keanna, to Crystal, to herself in the mirror, that it had begun to feel like memory rather than invention, and she understood now that she had been a sycophant for her own mythology, flattering it, feeding it grapes. She struck out the false paragraph. She could not absolve herself of the invention by crossing it out, and she did not try; she simply wrote, in the margin, in handwriting the stage lights would not forgive: he took the GED after the army. It was 1942 when they made it. He was prouder of that.

Her name was announced a full minute before she was ready for it. She climbed the stairs, shook the hand offered to her, accepted the folder that stood in for a diploma until the real one arrived by mail, and stepped to the microphone. The field went quiet except for a flag snapping somewhere behind the bleachers and Keanna, who was whistling with two fingers, badly and with love.

"My grandfather didn't finish high school the usual way," Katherine said. "He finished it in 1942, in the army, with a test they'd just made. I got my facts wrong about him this morning, and I'd like to get them right now." She looked out at the crooked rows, at her grandmother holding the program up like a small banner, and turned the page.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: Under US federal law, workers aged 16 and 17 have no limit on working hours but may not be employed in jobs the Department of Labor has declared hazardous.
story:
The playground behind the shuttered elementary school had become their office. Elijah sat on a swing that no longer swung, the chains rusted halfway up, and held his phone flat on his knees like a hymnal. On the screen were questions he had copied from a job interview website: Tell me about yourself. Describe a time you showed responsibility. Why do you want to work here? He was eighteen, broke, and had an interview Saturday morning at the garden center on Route 9, his first ever, and the thought of it made his voice disappear somewhere behind his sternum.

"You're doing the thing again," Mahdi said, hanging upside down from the monkey bars. "The staring-at-nothing thing."

"I practiced in the mirror last night. I looked like I was being interrogated."

Imane sat cross-legged at the top of the slide, the only one of them still small enough to fit there comfortably. "Practice on us. Mahdi, be the manager. Elijah, look at him when you answer. That's the whole assignment. Eye contact and clear answers. My sister says they decide in the first ninety seconds."

Mahdi dropped from the bars, dusted his hands on his jeans, and arranged his face into what he clearly believed was managerial authority. "So, Elijah. Why do you want this position?" He kept breaking into a grin, and Elijah kept looking at the woodchips, at the peeling paint of the slide, anywhere else, and Imane kept saying "eyes" like a metronome until Elijah wanted to walk home. It was Mahdi who finally cajoled him into one honest take, promising to buy him a slice after, promising to be serious, promising anything, and Elijah looked straight at him and said, "Because I need the money and I'm good at working hard, and I can prove both," and it came out steady, and Imane actually clapped.

Then, out of nowhere, Mahdi's phone buzzed and his whole posture changed. He read the message twice. "My manager wants me to close Friday and run the slicer," he said. "The meat slicer. Full shift."

"Is that allowed?" Imane asked. "You're seventeen."

"I can work as many hours as they give me. There's no limit at my age." Mahdi said it with the flat certainty of someone quoting something he'd been told, probably by the same manager. "Sixteen and seventeen, unlimited hours. That part I looked up when I started."

Elijah frowned. Something in that pairing bothered him, the way a word half-remembered bothers you. If there was no limit on hours, there was still something he'd read once, in a pamphlet or a footer of some website, a word that had stuck because it sounded biblical. "I don't think that's the whole rule," he said slowly. "Give me a second." He typed with his thumbs: can 17 year olds use meat slicer. The search results filled in faster than he expected.

Hazardous. That was the word. Jobs the Department of Labor had declared hazardous, and minors couldn't do them, and meat slicers were on that list. He read it twice and turned the phone so Mahdi could see. "So the hours thing is true, but there's a second half. Sixteen and seventeen, no limit on hours, but not in jobs the DOL has declared hazardous. The slicer counts. It's on the list."

From where Imane sat, the change in the light made the whole scene look like a painting, the three of them motionless around the small glowing screen. But it was Mahdi who felt the message rearrange itself inside him. He had been proud of that Friday shift, had already imagined telling his father, who believed that suffering built character and that Mahdi was too soft, an iconoclast in the house only when it came to his own son. Refusing a shift could look like exactly the softness his father expected. And yet there was the rule, plain as the rust on the swing chains, and the manager either didn't know it or hoped Mahdi didn't. Both possibilities were worse than the message itself.

"I'll text him I can close but not run the slicer," Mahdi said finally. "See what he says." He typed, deleted, typed again. Elijah watched him and understood something embryonic about himself, a shape he couldn't fully name yet: that the interview prep had never really been about eye contact. It was about this, about being the person who looks at the rule and the person and says the true thing without flinching. Or maybe it wasn't. Maybe he was just borrowing courage from a law that happened to be on his side.

"He's typing," Mahdi said.

Saturday morning, Elijah wore the one shirt with a collar and walked to the garden center with his hands sweating through the fabric. The manager, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, asked why he wanted the position, and Elijah looked directly at her and said he needed the money and was good at working hard and could prove both, and the sentence came out level, no grin breaking through his own face, no woodchips to study. She wrote something down. Behind her, through the window of the office, he could see the greenhouse, rows of seedlings in their embryonic leaves, and a forklift sitting parked by the loading dock, and he thought, absurdly, of slicers and hazardous lists and Mahdi still waiting for a reply.

"Do you have any questions for us?" the manager asked.

Elijah thought of Mahdi's unanswered text, of Imane clapping on the slide, of the swing that no longer swung. "One," he said, and held her eyes. "What would I actually be doing on a Saturday?"

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, launch angles that add up to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same range on level ground at the same speed.
story:
Gabriel had come to the skate park to do his physics homework, which everyone agreed was a strange place to do it, and which was exactly why he had come. The bowl's concrete curve rose around him like half of a giant pipe, and the paper on his knee kept threatening to blow away. He pinned it under his board. The problem was a ball launched at an angle, and he was supposed to find where it landed, which meant separating the velocity into a horizontal part and a vertical part, and he did not yet believe that such a thing was legal, taking one motion and cutting it into two.

"You're doing the thing with the arrows again," Ania said, dropping onto the ledge beside him. She had a water bottle and no homework, which was her usual arrangement.

"It's called components," Gabriel said. "Horizontal and vertical. They don't talk to each other. The sideways speed never changes, and the vertical speed gets pulled down by gravity, and if you keep them separate the whole time, you can solve for anything." He said it with more confidence than he had. He had copied the method from the board in Mr. Hughes's room that morning, and Mr. Hughes had said, almost as an aside, that angles that add up to ninety degrees would land a ball in the same spot on flat ground if you launched at the same speed. Gabriel had not believed him. Teachers said things like that the way weather reports said it might rain, and half the time the rain went elsewhere.

"Prove it," Ania said.

"You can't prove physics at a skate park."

Ania looked pointedly at the bowl, the smooth transitions, the pipes and rails, the whole engineered geometry of flight. "This is the most physics place in town."

Layla arrived before he could argue, carrying the small foam-ball launcher she had borrowed from the physics room without, she said, technically stealing it, since she intended to return it. She had heard them arguing from the top of the ramp. She sat down, set the launcher on the flat concrete at the park's edge where the ground was level, and cranked it to a fixed spring setting so the launch speed would be the same every time.

Gabriel took a piece of chalk from his pocket and drew a line on the ground. He was the one who had to know, so he was the one doing the work. He set the launcher at thirty degrees and fired. The orange ball climbed modestly, arced, and struck the concrete a good distance out. He marked the spot. Then he tilted the launcher up to sixty degrees and fired again. The ball went much higher, hung there in a way that felt theatrical, and came down.

It landed on the chalk mark. Not near it. On it.

Layla crouched over the mark. "Same spot."

"That's luck," Gabriel said, though he could feel the word losing its veracity even as he said it. They fired each angle again, and again, and the two balls kept landing in the same place, the shallow fast one and the high slow one, as if they had agreed on it in the air. He thought of Mr. Hughes saying it that morning, offhand, almost bored, and felt the small shame of having decided the man was wrong without checking. He had a habit of that, he admitted to himself now, titrating his respect for people based on how confident they sounded rather than whether they were right, and the mixture came out wrong more often than he liked.

He got out the homework problem again. The launch angle was thirty degrees, and the ball came out at twenty meters per second. He drew the arrows. Ten times the square root of three going sideways, untouched by gravity, and ten going straight up, which gravity would grind down to zero and then reverse. Separate them. Keep them separate. Time came from the vertical part, distance from the horizontal part, and when he put them back together the answer fell out, whole and clean. The recalcitrant problem, which had resisted him all week, had only been refusing to be solved all at once.

He thought of his father, who fixed cars and distrusted anything you couldn't hold, saying that school physics was just arithmetic wearing a costume. Gabriel had half believed him. He looked at the two chalk marks, the single spot where two opposite trajectories agreed, and understood that his father was also not wrong, exactly, only looking at it from one angle, the way Gabriel had been looking at the whole problem from one angle. Two people could aim very differently and still arrive at the same place. He didn't know yet what to do with that thought. He filed it next to the uneaten feeling about Mr. Hughes.

"Again," Layla said, cranking the launcher. "But this time you call it."

"Seventy degrees," Gabriel said, already chalking a new line beside the mark.

"Then I get twenty," said Ania, and she put her sneaker on the chalk spot to hold it.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: In Marxist terms, the bourgeoisie owns the means of production, such as factories and land, while the proletariat owns only its labour and must sell it for wages.
story:
Charlotte arrived at the book club meeting carrying Jane Eyre, a highlighted photocopy, and the private suspicion that Ms. Aziz had invented the assignment specifically to ruin her Saturday. The task, written on the board in Ms. Aziz's slanted hand, was to read a passage "through a Marxist lens," and Charlotte had spent the bus ride staring at Thornfield Hall in the rain, feeling nothing but mild sympathy for the roofers.

"There she is," said Laurence, who had claimed the good chair and was guarding a plate of biscuits. "Did you do the reading or are we about to witness improvisation?"

"I did the reading. I also understood maybe forty percent of it." She dropped into the seat beside him. "The passage is where Jane says she's a free human being with an independent will, right before agreeing to work for wages for a man who owns a giant house. I feel like the lens is supposed to make that ironic, but every time I try to say how, it comes out like a fortune cookie."

Braiden spun a marker and stood at the whiteboard like a game show host. "Okay, sorting time. Owners on the left, workers on the right. Rochester," and he wrote it on the left, "because house, land, the whole estate. Mrs. Fairfax on the right. Jane on the right. Adele, tiny child, right, purely on vibes."

"The left is the people who own the means of production," Laurence said, chewing a biscuit. "The right is everyone else."

Charlotte looked at the board. "Everyone else being...?"

"The people who own nothing except their labour," Braiden said, "and have to sell it for wages. That's the whole arrangement. It's called the proletariat, by the way, and the owners are the bourgeoisie. Congratulations, you now know two French words."

"Which I could have learned from a bakery sign," Charlotte said, but she was copying the board into her notebook, and something was assembling itself, the way a puzzle does when enough sky is in place that the birds become obvious. Jane owned her opinions, her stubbornness, her tiny suitcase, and nothing else. She walked to Thornfield and sold her days the way anyone sold anything, because the alternative was not walking anywhere. Her famous declaration of independence was true in one way and, laid against the whiteboard, not true in another, and the interesting thing was that Charlotte had never had to hold both of those at once before.

"I think I have something," she said, and stood up. "It's not that Jane's wrong. It's that the book lets her speak like she's free while the plot keeps her in the right-hand column. So the Marxist lens isn't calling her a liar. It's pointing out that the freedom she describes can't actually be exercised, because she has to sell her labour and Rochester doesn't have to sell anything, so his version of the same feelings costs him less." She heard herself and winced. "That sounded smarter in my head. And also more British."

"It sounded pretty good," said Laurence. "Braiden's going to argue now, because it's Braiden."

"I'm only going to argue a little," Braiden said, capping the marker. "What about Jane's inheritance at the end? She moves to the left column. Doesn't that break your whole reading?"

Charlotte opened her mouth, closed it, and studied the board, where the columns sat there being smug. "It complicates it. The book solves her problem by making her an owner instead of by changing the arrangement, which might be the most revealing part. But I can't tell if that's a real insight or sophistry with good posture." She glanced at Ms. Aziz, who had been quiet at the window in a way Charlotte suspected was deliberate, and who now raised her eyebrows as if to say, go on, fall or don't. "Okay, here's what I actually think. The lens works. It shows something the plain reading hides. What I can't decide is whether it explains the book or just re-describes it in worse sentences. Is that a tenable position, having a lens and doubting it at the same time?"

"It's the only tenable position," said Laurence. "If you never doubted your lens, your brain would atrophy and we'd have to bury it in the garden."

"That's not how brains work."

"It's how brains work," Braiden said solemnly. "I've seen it."

Ms. Aziz finally spoke. "Write it down before it dissolves into biscuits," she said, nodding at Charlotte's notebook. "The doubt, especially. That's the part most people throw away."

Charlotte wrote: the lens reveals, the inheritance complicates, the doubt stays. Then she added, in smaller letters, ask about the feminist lens next week, because Jane's speech had a second life in it too, and turned the notebook toward Laurence. "Read that back to me. Tell me if I sound like a person or a fortune cookie."

He squinted at the page. "Sixty percent person," he said. "Personal best."

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five 'filters', the first of which is the ownership of media by large corporations.
story:
The newspaper office smelled of toner and old carpet, and the radiator under the window ticked like something counting. Xavier had claimed the desk by the filing cabinet because it was the only one where the chair didn't wobble, and he was laying out the front page when Ayesha dropped a book on top of his layout grids.

"You have to read this," she said. "It's for Ms. Wardak's class. Manufacturing Consent, Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky, 1988. I keep seeing it everywhere I look now."

"Everywhere where?" Kiley asked from the copier, which was making its slow, asthmatic run through the back-page proofs.

"Like, who owns the things I read." Ayesha pulled the book toward her and opened it to a page she'd already marked with a receipt. "They argue news is shaped by five filters. Five. And the first one is ownership. Media owned by large corporations." She said it flat, the way she recited stats for debate, then closed the book. "That's the whole first filter. I didn't even know outlets had owners, really. Or I knew and never thought about it."

Xavier smoothed the grid back out under the book's edge. He was seventeen and had been editor of the Ledger for one year, and in that year he had thought mostly about fonts and deadlines and whether the vice principal would spike the story about the parking lot repaving contract. The idea that a paper could be shaped by whoever owned it felt like weather: real, distant, not his problem. Except that his problem, this week, was exactly the parking lot contract.

"Here's the thing," he said. He pulled the folder from his backpack and spread the pages on the desk between them. "The district accepted a bid from Halloran Paving. The lowest bid was twelve thousand dollars cheaper, from a company nobody's heard of. And Halloran's regional VP is on the school board's facilities committee. Not voting on it, just, on the committee. I've been sitting on this for two weeks."

Kiley came over wiping toner from her fingers with the hem of her sweatshirt. "Sitting on it why?"

"Because I can't figure out if it's a story or if it's me seeing filters everywhere like Ayesha." He said the word carefully, trying it out. "Nothing here is owned by a corporation. We're a school paper. We have a faculty adviser and a budget of four hundred dollars from the activity fund."

"The adviser reports to the principal," Ayesha said. "And the principal reports to the board."

The radiator ticked. Somewhere down the hall a janitor's cart squeaked past, and the fluorescent light above the copier buzzed in a register Xavier had long since stopped hearing until moments like this, when the room went quiet enough for it to matter. He looked at the bid documents, the numbers lined up in columns, and then at the mock-up of the front page, where his lead story was about the fall play. The play was safe. The play was the kind of thing he'd been trained, without anyone ever saying it aloud, to put first.

He had learned, somewhere in his junior year, to compartmentalize: the Ledger was one drawer, school politics another, and the two never touched. Ayesha's book suggested the drawers were false. What he wanted, sitting there under the buzzing light, was to hold both thoughts at once without pretending either one was simple. He even knew the word for watching his own thinking from a little distance; Ms. Wardak had written it on the board the first week of term, metacognition, and told them that knowing a bias existed was not the same as escaping it.

"Let's say I write it," he said. "Accurate, both bids quoted, the committee membership confirmed. What happens?"

"Ms. Wardak reads it before print," Kiley said. "That's the policy."

"She reads it. She doesn't kill it. That's the adviser's job, and she's never killed anything." Xavier tapped the folder. "But it goes to the principal's office after. And the principal plays golf with the facilities chair, probably, or whatever the indoor equivalent of golf is. And next semester our budget comes up for renewal."

"So you're the corporation," Ayesha said. It wasn't a joke, quite, and it wasn't accusation either. She sat on the edge of the desk, which the desk was not built for, and looked at the proof pages like they were something from an obsolescent era, a museum of a thing that had once believed in itself.

"That's the part I can't decide," Xavier said. "If I don't run it because I'm worried about the budget, that's the filter, working exactly like the book says. If I run it just to prove I can, that's not journalism either, that's me wanting to be the kind of person who runs things. I don't know which one I'm doing. I genuinely don't."

Nobody answered. The copier finished its run and shut itself off with a sigh, and the room became very quiet, the kind of quiet where the tick of the radiator sounded deliberate. Kiley gathered the back-page proofs and squared them against the table, twice, though they were already even.

"Write it tonight," she said. "I'll copy-edit. If Wardak flags anything, we fix it, and then you decide with her, out loud, on the record, what the paper can stand behind." She handed Ayesha the toner-smudged stack to collate, then pulled Xavier's chair out from the desk and rolled it toward him across the worn carpet.

He sat, opened a blank document, and typed the first line of the story, and in the window behind him the parking lot went on gleaming, black and freshly sealed, under the October sun.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they keep December 25 on the older Julian calendar.
story:
The park had been loaned to them for the afternoon, and Matthew's grandmother had claimed a picnic table near the frozen duck pond, spreading a cloth over the slats as though it were July. Around them, families unpacked kutchie and honey cake and thermoses of tea, and someone had strung a line of white bulbs between two oaks, unlit until dusk. It was January seventh, which was Christmas, a fact Matthew had explained twice already that morning and which still made him feel like he was translating something that lost power in the crossing.

"Your Christmas is late," said his little cousin, with the pugnacious certainty of an eight-year-old who has found what looks like a weakness in an older boy.

"It's not late," Matthew said. "It's on time for us."

"Brooke said nobody has Christmas in January."

"Brooke," Matthew said, "has never met my grandmother."

He said it lightly, but the conversation followed him across the park, the way things did when you were sixteen and half of you wanted to stand up for the old ways and the other half wanted to be the kind of person for whom nothing needed defending. His father had grown up in this, the midnight service, the fasting that ended at the star appearing; Matthew had grown up in both worlds, the December of his friends and the January of his family, and he had never quite decided whether that made him rich or divided.

He found Mackenna at the hot chocolate stand, holding two cups, one clearly meant for him. She was in his history class, the class autodidact, the girl who read footnotes for pleasure and had once corrected a documentary in front of everyone.

"So this is the real thing," she said, handing him the cup. "I looked it up last night. Many Orthodox churches, including the Russian Orthodox Church, celebrate Christmas on January seventh, because they keep December twenty-fifth on the older Julian calendar." She said it the way she said everything, as a gift, not a correction. "So when your neighbors tore down their trees two weeks ago, yours was still standing."

"I didn't know that part," Matthew admitted. "The calendar part. I just knew we did it now."

"That's the best part, though. It's not a different holiday. It's the same date on a different calendar." She sipped her chocolate. "Your grandmother kept December twenty-fifth. Just not the one printed on your phone."

Matthew looked back toward the picnic table, where his grandmother was pouring tea for a woman from the church choir, both of them laughing about something in Russian that he could half follow. His whole life he had assumed the January date was simply theirs, a family quirk like his grandmother's habit of refusing to sit with her back to a door. It had never occurred to him that it was an argument, a position, that somewhere in the history there had been a choice and people who refused to unmake it.

"There's a boy at my school," Mackenna went on, watching a group of younger kids attempt to slide across the pond's thin ice, "who told me your family was just wrong. He said the date is the date."

"And what did you say?"

"I said calendars are just agreements." She shrugged. "Though I'm not sure that's true either. Somebody has to be keeping better time."

The service was to begin at four, in the field house the park had also loaned them, and the priest was setting up near the door, an old man with a beard white as the frost. Matthew's cousin came running up with an armful of paper stars for the children to carry, and when Mackenna tried to interpose herself between the boy and the pond, explaining that the ice would not hold him, he dodged around her with the paper stars flaring like small fires in his fists.

"He's fine," Matthew said. "It froze solid last week."

"You don't know that."

"I don't," he agreed, and found that the admission cost him something small and gave him something back. His whole afternoon had been like that. Mackenna, who believed in dates and documents, had handed him a fact that let him see his grandmother's January as a kind of fidelity rather than a delay, and yet the fact also widened the distance: now he knew the name of the thing that separated his family's Christmas from Brooke's, and a named distance is harder to ignore than an unexplained one.

The little cousin reached the pond and slid out onto the ice, wobbling, arms out, a paper star in each hand, and he did not fall. The kids on the far bank cheered. Mackenna exhaled beside Matthew, half relief, half reluctance, the way one watches a thing succeed that one had argued against.

"They're starting," his grandmother called, waving him toward the field house, and the white bulbs between the oaks came on all at once, pale in the daylight, burning anyway.

"Can I come in?" Mackenna asked. "Just to see?"

"Bring the chocolate," Matthew said, and they walked toward the singing.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: In his 1865 book The Coal Question, William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use and increased Britain's total coal consumption.
story:
The photocopy of the utility bill was warm from the copier, and Kaylee smoothed it flat on the lab bench before anyone could see her hands. The environmental club met in Room 114 on Thursdays, the chemistry lab with its faint smell of sulfur and lemon disinfectant, and today the windows were open because the radiator clanked even in April. Marley arrived first, as always, balancing a stack of the LED fundraiser order forms. Calla came in late with wet hair and the particular look of someone who had run from the far parking lot.

"Before anyone gets excited," Kaylee said, "look at this."

She slid the bill across the bench. It was the school's, October through March, printed in the thin gray ink of a district office printer. Six months ago the club had finished replacing every hallway and classroom bulb with LEDs, the project they had petitioned for at two school board meetings, the project Ms. Das had signed off on with her careful signature. The bulbs used a fraction of the electricity of the old ones. Everyone had said so, including the packaging.

Marley frowned at the numbers. "That can't be right. We're using more power than last year."

"That's what I thought. So I got the other bills." Kaylee pulled the rest of the photocopies from her backpack, the whole year, October to October, two sets so they could compare. She laid them side by side, the old year on top, the new year below, and ran her finger down the kilowatt-hour column. The numbers did not argue. Usage was up eleven percent, and the year before that, up again.

Calla leaned in, pushing wet hair off her forehead. "Maybe they estimated the meter."

"I called. They came and read it."

The door opened and Ms. Das came in with her mug and her roll book, and the room shifted into its ordinary Thursday rhythm for a moment, the radiator knocking, a lawnmower somewhere outside going back and forth. Kaylee watched Ms. Das take attendance without really seeing her, because she was thinking about the middle of the winter bill, December, the month the usage had jumped hardest, and she was not ready to say what she had noticed yet, because if she said it out loud and it was stupid, Calla would remember it forever.

"Ms. Das," she said instead, "do we have any book in the library about the history of energy? Not solar panels. History."

Ms. Das considered her over the mug. "There's a shelf in the back corner. Old economics texts, mostly donations. Try there before I shelve them." That was all she said, and Kaylee was grateful, because a speech would have made it worse.

The library at 3:40 was in its quiescent hour, the after-school crowd gone and the evening crowd not yet arrived, the light through the tall windows laying long yellow rectangles across the carpet. Kaylee found the shelf, warped and smelling of dust, and worked along it with her finger. She had a half-memory, something she had read at her uncle's apartment last summer while it rained, a sentence that had seemed boring then and seemed important now. The books delimited the whole question, she thought, from firewood to uranium, and somewhere in the middle of them was the sentence she wanted. She found it in a fat brown volume, a chapter about coal, and she stood in the aisle reading it twice.

In 1865, in a book called The Coal Question, William Stanley Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made coal cheaper to use and increased Britain's total coal consumption. She read the line again. Cheaper to use, and more coal burned, not less. The opposite of what everyone promised.

She carried the book back to Room 114 at a pace that was almost not running. Calla and Marley were still there, counting fundraiser money into coin rolls, and Ms. Das was erasing the board with slow strokes.

"Listen," Kaylee said, and read the sentence aloud, holding the book open with her thumb. "Eighteen sixty-five. Steam engines. Britain burned more coal, not less, after the engines got efficient."

Marley squinted. "That's the opposite of us."

"No," Kaylee said, and this was the part she had worked out on the walk back, the part she still wasn't sure of, and she said it anyway. "It's exactly us. Look at December." She spread the bills again. "December is when the district added the evening program. Night classes, the gym open till ten, the parking lot lights on a new schedule. The LEDs made the electricity so cheap to run that nobody thought twice about leaving everything on. The bulbs aren't the problem. The cheapness is."

Calla sat back. "So we did all that work so the school could afford to use more?"

"I don't know," Kaylee said. "Not exactly. It's not like we shouldn't have switched. It's that switching wasn't the whole thing, and everyone acted like it was." She heard how unsure she sounded and let it stand, because the alternative was pretending, and she had watched two years of pretending produce these bills.

Ms. Das had stopped erasing. "So what do you want to do?"

Kaylee looked at the numbers, at the December spike, at the book still open on the bench with its 1865 sentence, at the windows going amber with late sun. "I want to ask the board why the gym lights run till ten when the gym closes at eight. And I want to find out before I ask, so nobody can tell me it's a scheduling thing."

Calla snapped a coin roll shut. "Then we're going back through the security logs tonight. My mom works in the front office until six."

Kaylee closed the book, and the three of them walked out together into the long liminality of the empty hallway, half day and half not yet night, where the new bulbs burned steadily above them, every single one of them on.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
