knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
Maya carried the crate of tomatoes across the farmers' market and tried not to think about the empty chair at the kitchen table. Her mother had said, that morning, that Sunday dinner would go on as usual, which meant Maya was cooking it, because her mother had taken an extra shift at the hospital and wouldn't be home until ten. Somewhere between the bread stall and the honey vendor, Maya had promised herself a proper meal, the kind her grandmother used to make, and now she was standing at the egg stand watching a boy from her chemistry class, Maximilien, stack cartons.

"You're buying two dozen," he said. "Who are you feeding?"

"My family. It's complicated." She counted out coins, and then, because he was there and it was easier than carrying the thought alone, she added, "I'm making my grandmother's Sunday chicken. She's in the hospital too, same one as my mom works at. Different floor."

Maximilien didn't say anything sentimental, which she appreciated. He said, "Then you need good eggs," and slid the darkest carton toward her. At the next stall Nola was arguing with a vendor about whether the garlic was local, holding up a bulb like a pundit holding up evidence, declaring its provenance suspect. Nola had been accepted to a politics program in the fall and had grown fond of cross-examining everyone, including garlic.

At home, the kitchen smelled of thyme and hot oil, and the chicken was browning nicely, its skin beginning to burnish in the pan. Maya set the tomatoes out, sliced bread, and started the mayonnaise, because her grandmother's chicken demanded it, a pale bowl of it for dragging each bite through. She had watched her grandmother make it a hundred times, one yolk, a whisk, oil in a thin slow stream. She whisked and poured the way she remembered, and for a while the mixture turned thick and glossy and right.

Then it split. She didn't know what she had done wrong, only that the bowl had gone from satin to something loose and curdled, yellow liquid swimming with a slick of oil on top, and no amount of whisking pulled it back together. She stood at the counter with her phone in her hand, ready to text her mother, and put it down. Her mother would be in the middle of a shift. She texted Nola instead, sent a photo of the ruined bowl, and got back a string of exclamation points and the suggestion to throw it out and start over.

Maya didn't want to start over. It felt like the wrong answer to the right question. She called her grandmother's room, and a nurse held the phone close, and her grandmother's voice came through thin but entirely itself. Maya described what she'd done, and her grandmother asked a single question: had she added the oil too fast at the end? Maya looked at the measuring cup, nearly empty, and admitted she probably had, because the bread was waiting and she'd hurried.

"You broke it, that's all," her grandmother said. "The lecithin and the proteins in the yolk are the emulsifiers. They hold the tiny oil droplets suspended in the water so the sauce doesn't separate. You outran them." Then, before Maya could apologize, she said, "Start a fresh yolk in a clean bowl. Beat it, then slowly whisk the broken sauce into it." There was a pause, some murmur in the room behind her, and then she said, "Slowly this time, Maya. Tell your mother I want the leftovers saved."

Maya cracked a new yolk into a clean bowl and whisked until it ribboned, then added the failed sauce a teaspoon at a time, her wrist aching, the oil-veined liquid folding in and thickening, becoming mayonnaise again, smooth and complete. She stood over it feeling something she didn't have a word for, part relief and part something more cerebral, the specific satisfaction of understanding a thing instead of only repeating it. She had thought cooking was memory; it turned out it was also chemistry, and the two were not rivals but the same act described in different languages, one by her grandmother's hands and one by a textbook she would meet in the fall.

Nola and Maximilien arrived just before seven with more bread than anyone needed, and they ate in the kitchen with the windows open, dragging chicken through the rescued mayonnaise. Maya's mother texted that she'd gotten the message about leftovers and would stop by her own mother's floor before coming home. It was not the Sunday they used to have, and Maya didn't pretend to herself that one bowl of sauce fixed anything. But when Maximilien asked for the recipe, she found herself saying she'd have to show him, because the showing was the whole of it, and she set the extra carton of eggs on the counter where she could see them.

"Tomorrow," Nola said, already slicing more bread. "Same time. I'll bring the garlic."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it.
story:
The binder Mr. Yip handed out had a week of empty boxes on one side and the word REST printed across Saturday in a font so large it looked like a warning. Madison sat on the bleachers in the school gym with her knees drawn up, tracing the boxes with a pencil. First practice of the season was Monday, and she was supposed to fill the week in before it started: drills, warm-ups, a day of nothing. A day of nothing felt like a lie you told people who were weaker than you, and she did not think of herself as one of those people.

"You're staring at that like it's a ransom note," said Madyson, dropping onto the bench beside her. Madyson, whose parents had apparently never met a y before adding one, had been Madison's partner in every group project since grade nine, mostly because teachers got tired of saying both names aloud. "Just write running in every box. That's what I did."

"That's not a program," Madison said. "That's a slogan." But she wrote something close to it anyway, because the empty boxes were worse than the wrong ones. Monday, sprints. Tuesday, sprints. Wednesday, more sprints, and she pencilled a small arrow beside Saturday's REST that said maybe.

Soren, stretched out along the bleachers with his shoe off, inspecting a blister, leaned over to look. "You're going to do legs three days in a row and then run Sunday?" he asked. "Bold. Malevolent, even." He said the last word the way he said most words, half as a joke and entirely as a fact. Madison pulled the binder away from him, though the remark settled somewhere under her ribs and stayed there.

Monday's practice left her feeling suspiciously fine. She had expected to feel like a conquered city by evening, and instead she walked home light, almost smug, and texted Madyson that the program was working. Madyson replied with a thumbs up and the message "I can barely move, you mutant." Madison decided her friend was simply not a serious person, possibly a hedonist, and went to sleep proud.

Wednesday morning she woke to legs that had been replaced overnight with something heavy and punitive. Stairs became a negotiation. She sat down in the gym at lunch, winced getting there, and pulled out her phone, typing with the vague hope that the internet would confirm she had a rare condition. Instead the first result told her something she had never thought to wonder about: soreness like this usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it. She read the line twice. It had not lied in wait and then ambushed her; it had simply arrived on its own schedule, like a bill. All those times she had felt fine after a hard practice and concluded she was invincible, the evidence had merely been on its way.

She found Mr. Yip after last period, by the equipment cage, and asked whether that was true, the 24 to 72 hours thing, the peak coming days later instead of right after. "Delayed-onset muscle soreness," he said, and went back to counting cones, which was the most anyone could hope for from him. She carried the phrase out of the gym like contraband. So the fine feeling on Monday had been a trick of timing, and Madyson, unable to move, had been the accurate one. It was almost funny, if you were the kind of person who could laugh while lowering yourself onto a chair with both hands on the armrests.

On Thursday she rewrote the week in the binder. Monday, drills, moderate, with the full warm-up she had skipped because warm-ups were for people who planned badly. Tuesday, something upper body, which felt embarrassingly sensible. Wednesday, easy. Saturday, REST, the capital letters intact, no arrow, no maybe. She had wanted to believe that effort paid instantly, and that rest was for the unserious, and the truth seemed to be that the body kept its own ledger and settled accounts days later. Whether one hard day or two moderate ones built more speed, she still could not say; she had a guess and a chart and a set of very sore legs, and only one of those was evidence.

Friday, walking almost normally, she showed Madyson the new program. Madyson studied it, nodded slowly, and then said, "So what you're telling me is I should prevaricate less and stretch more," which was not what the word meant, and Madison told her so at length. They were still arguing about it when Soren came up the hallway, moving with the careful, ceremonial slowness of a much older man, one hand on the wall.

"Sprints Monday," he said. "Can barely walk today."

"Give it until tomorrow," Madison said, and held the gym door open for him.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: In the United States, most negative information on a credit report, such as late payments, can be reported for seven years, and bankruptcies for up to ten.
story:
The folder in Jackson's hand had grown thick by noon, full of flyers for programs he could not name an hour earlier, and the credit card booth near the dining hall doors had a better giveaway than any of them: a water bottle with the bank's logo, free the moment you filled out an application. Barrett had already filled his out, pen moving fast, mostly for the bottle, partly because the recruiter had called him "sir."

"Approved in sixty seconds," Barrett said, holding up his phone. "I feel like an adult. I feel like a man with a water bottle and a credit limit."

"You already have a credit card," Elise said. She was standing with the loose patience of someone waiting for a friend to finish being wrong. "Your dad's, the one with your name on it. You missed the payment on it last month. You told me."

"It was thirty dollars. Dad paid it like two weeks later."

Jackson had been half listening, weighing the water bottle against the form, and now he set both on the table without signing anything. Elise turned to the recruiter, a grad student working the booth for twenty dollars an hour and clearly bored of enthusiasm, and asked how long a late payment stayed on a report.

"Seven years," the recruiter said, not looking up from her phone. "Most negative stuff on a credit report, seven years. Bankruptcy's worse, up to ten."

"Ten," Barrett repeated. "Years."

"Years," she said, and finally looked at him. "You want the bottle anyway? They're not going to chase you."

Barrett took the bottle. He turned it over in his hands like evidence. "So a payment I missed when I was seventeen follows me until I'm twenty-four. I could be married. I could have a kid. The kid will hear about the thirty dollars."

"That's not how it works," Elise said, but she didn't say how it did work, because none of them knew, and the recruiter had gone back to her phone.

They walked on toward the economics building, where Elise wanted the tour, because Elise wanted the economics building the way other people wanted concerts. She had a plan involving internships, a Roth IRA she had opened at sixteen, and a spreadsheet she described with real affection. Jackson followed because the tour was on his list too, and because Barrett kept holding the bottle at arm's length as if it might go off.

Inside, a professor was talking to a cluster of parents about the labor market, and the word "stagflation" drifted out of the lecture hall, flat and alarming. One of the mothers audibly gasped. "It means prices and unemployment rise together while growth stalls," the professor said, "though I'd rather you heard it from me than from the evening news." Jackson filed the word away with the others he had collected that day, a pocketful of small heavy stones.

What he could not file was the seven years. On the tour, while the guide pointed out a computer lab and a wall of founders' photos, Jackson did the arithmetic against his own life. He would graduate in four. Two years after that, the number seven would still have three left on it, whatever he had signed or skipped signing at eighteen. It was not that the water bottle was a trap; it was that the person who wanted the water bottle and the person who would want an apartment in 2033 were strangers to each other, connected only by the paperwork. Barrett was learning this through a thirty-dollar mistake. Elise had apparently learned it before she could drive. Jackson had learned it standing at a folding table, and he was still deciding what it was worth.

Barrett had gone quiet, which was rare enough that Elise checked on him. "You're not actually going to name a kid after a late fee," she said.

"I'm thinking about my dad. He missed that payment because of the hospital thing in March, and it's on his report too, for seven years, and nobody in that booth mentioned it. It's like they hand you a bottle of water and don't tell you the water's tracking you."

"That's a terrible metaphor," Elise said, "but I take your point."

After the tour there was a breakout session with a financial aid officer, a Ms. Liu, who took questions in a room where the air conditioning had been off all morning and the folder pages had begun to curl and desiccate in Jackson's grip. He asked about student cards, whether they helped or hurt, and Ms. Liu said only, "That depends on the person holding it," which was either useless or the truest thing anyone had said all day. Barrett asked whether his dad could get the late payment removed, and Ms. Liu said disputes existed but she couldn't advise on private accounts, and offered him a mint from a tin on the table, which he accepted like a consolation prize.

Outside, on the steps of the building, Jackson took out the blank application he had pocketed without meaning to. He looked down the quad at the booths, the balloons, the future being handed out in swag. He thought: the canny move is to build credit early and carefully, and the honest move is to admit I don't yet trust myself with a Wednesday night and a pizza impulse. Both could be true. He folded the application in half, then in quarters, and put it in his back pocket instead of the trash, which was a decision that looked like nothing and felt like something.

"I'm going to apply," Barrett said, from beside him, still holding the bottle. "But I'm setting every alert the app has. Daily alerts. Hourly. The payment's due and a man should know."

"Setting alerts," Elise said. "Look at him grow."

Jackson unfolded the paper a quarter of the way, then folded it back. "Not today," he said, and lifted his folder like a shield against the sun coming off the steps.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Compound interest follows A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where n is how many times per year interest is added, so more frequent compounding gives a slightly larger total.
story:
Justine had forty-one dollars in her backpack, folded into an envelope she'd made from a worksheet on the French Revolution, and she intended to walk it straight into the credit union on Haldane Street before Lane could talk her out of it. She'd been talking herself out of it for three weeks, which was the trouble. Every Friday she cleaned Mr. Okafor's gutters and took his twenty dollars, and every Friday the twenty dollars evaporated, mostly into milkshakes, once into a ceramic frog she'd bought to make Lane laugh and then had to hide from her mother, who considered ceramic frogs a symptom of weak character.

Lane was waiting by the bike rack outside the bank, which meant she'd timed it, which meant she wanted something. "Before you go in there," Lane said, "I need you to hear my plan."

"You want to borrow money."

"Forty dollars. For the amp." Lane played bass in a band with Melodie and two boys Justine didn't trust, and the band had one working amp between them. "I'll pay you back by December. With, like, interest. Whatever the bank does, I'll do that."

Inside, the credit union smelled like carpet cleaner and free coffee, and a woman at a desk by the window waved them over before Justine could decide whether to be nervous. Ms. Eze had a name tag and a dish of mints and, it turned out, opinions. When Justine slid the envelope across and said she wanted to start saving, Ms. Eze pulled up two accounts on her screen and turned it so Justine could read.

"Same rate on both," Ms. Eze said. "But look here. This one compounds monthly. This one, yearly."

Justine read the small print twice. "So the monthly one gives you more?"

"A slightly larger total, yes." Ms. Eze spun the dish of mints once, like a wheel. "It's called compounding, the way interest gets added and then earns interest itself. You seem like a girl who wants the slightly larger total."

"I do," Justine said, and was surprised by how much she did. On the walk over it had felt like a gesture, forty-one dollars surrendered to a beige building. Now it felt like setting a mousetrap for the future. She wondered whether her grandmother, who kept cash in a coffee tin and called bankers charlatans, had ever stood in a room like this and seen the numbers lined up on a screen. Probably not. Probably the coffee tin was a whole philosophy, and here was Justine, eighteen minutes into hers.

Lane was meanwhile discovering the loan side of the building, where a poster explained that borrowed money also accrued interest, and that a $500 loan paid back slowly could cost noticeably more than $500. She came back holding a pamphlet like it was evidence at a trial. "So if I borrow from you at bank rates, I owe you more than forty dollars. And if you'd just put the forty in the account, it would have grown. Either way I'm the boreal end of this arrangement. The cold end."

"That's not what boreal means," Justine said, though she liked the sound of it, forests of spruce, the far north of a friendship.

"I'm using it artistically."

Ms. Eze, who had clearly been listening with the serene patience of a woman who had watched a thousand teenagers argue near her mints, said only, "The monthly one is a good choice," and printed the form.

The trouble was this: Justine could hold both ideas at once, and neither one won. Lane would pay her back, probably, eventually, with a version of interest she'd calculate wrong and then defend passionately. But the forty dollars, left alone in the monthly account, would do its quiet multiplying without anyone's friendship on the line, and Justine had just learned that more frequent compounding gave a slightly larger total, and something about that phrase had gotten into her. Slightly larger. It wasn't a promise of riches. It was a promise of direction. She liked knowing which way a thing drifted when you weren't watching it. What she couldn't yet say was whether it was wiser to protect the drift or to bet on Lane, who was standing there with the pamphlet crushed in one hand, actually reading it now, actually frowning.

"I changed my mind," Lane said, which was rare enough that Justine looked up. "About the amp. Ask Melodie's cousin. He's got one in his basement and he only charges nachos." She set the crushed pamphlet on the edge of Ms. Eze's desk, smoothing it flat, an apology of the kind Lane knew how to make. "Your money should sit in there and do its little math."

Justine signed the form with the bank's chained pen, and Ms. Eze stamped something, and outside the light had gone the flat gray of late afternoon. Lane straddled her bike. "Forty-one dollars," she said. "In a year you'll have, what, forty-one dollars and a nickel?"

"A slightly larger total," Justine said. "Than that. Probably."

"Probably," Lane agreed, and pushed off toward Melodie's house, ringing her bell twice for no reason at all.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
Nathaniel had claimed the burner by the window before anyone else could, because the light there was honest. In the school cooking classroom, under Ms. Wijaya's supervision, the seniors were each preparing one dish to take home for a family dinner, and his mother had asked for nothing except "something sweet, something you made yourself." He had said he'd bring caramel sauce. She hadn't asked what he'd pour it over, and he hadn't said, and that unfinished sentence had sat between them all week like a cup nobody would pick up.

He set the pan on the heat and added only sugar, nothing else, because a video he'd watched at two in the morning had insisted that water was optional and stirring was a sin. Behind him, Caleb was browning chicken with the volume of someone performing bravery, and Jack was reading a thermometer like it owed him money.

"You're not adding butter?" Jack said, drifting over. "Every recipe I've seen starts with butter."

"Butter has proteins. It browns differently." Nathaniel watched the white crystals at the edges begin to slacken. "The sugar has to do this part alone."

"Alone how?"

Before Nathaniel could answer, the smell of burning chicken crossed the room and Caleb swore and lunged for his pan, and Ms. Wijaya's voice carried over the fans: "Caleb, lower the heat or lose the fond." The moment folded itself away. Nathaniel turned back to his own work.

He had brought his notebook, the black one from English, because caramel was one of the few things that rewarded both patience and precision. On the left-hand pages he kept what he'd read: caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins, and table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius. On the right-hand pages he kept what he'd done, and so far the right side said only, "Waited. Nothing happened. Waited more."

The sugar melted from the outside in, clearing to a liquid like weak tea, and nothing browned, and he began to ruminate on the possibility that two in the morning videos were a munificent source of confidence and a poor source of instruction. He thought about his mother's face when he'd said he'd make something. He thought about the philosophy elective he'd signed up for in the fall, the one his father called expensive navel-gazing and Jack called "basically existentialism with a syllabus," and how both of them somehow wanted the same thing from him, which was for him to stop talking about it and be something.

"Check your thermometer," Jack said, back at his shoulder. "One sixty-two."

Nathaniel wiped the probe and dipped it. The reading climbed slowly, 165, 168, and the liquid stayed pale, and he understood at last that the number he'd written down was not a caution but a promise. Sugar browned on its own, without proteins, and it began at about 170 degrees, and until then there was nothing to do but wait and not stir and not panic. He held still.

"One seventy-one," Jack read. "One seventy-three."

The color turned in the space of a breath, amber flooding outward from the center like ink in water, and Nathaniel's whole body wanted to lift the pan immediately. Burnt was one flip of a second away; he'd seen the warnings. But pale caramel tasted of nothing but sweet, and he did not want to bring his mother something that tasted of nothing.

"Take it off," Jack said.

"One more second."

"You're going to burn it."

"One more." The amber deepened toward copper, glossy as varnish, and at the exact moment he decided he could no longer tell courage from recklessness, he slid the pan off the heat and poured in the cream he'd warmed. The sauce roared up, hissed, settled. He stirred, and it went smooth and the color of dark honey.

Ms. Wijaya passed behind them, looked into the pan, and looked longer than she usually bothered. "Deep amber," she said. "Braver than most of them go." She moved on to rescue Caleb's fond.

Nathaniel spooned a little onto a plate and let it cool, and when he touched it to his tongue it tasted of heat and sugar and something almost bitter underneath, a flavor with a shadow to it. Jack tasted it too and said nothing, which from Jack was a review.

"You told me to take it off," Nathaniel said.

"You told yourself not to."

They cleaned the station mostly in silence, the way they did after anything that had gone right, and Caleb came over finally, plate of chicken in hand, and said, "So what do I do with this at home?" and Nathaniel looked at the jar of sauce cooling by the window, sealed and labeled in his own handwriting, and thought of setting it down on his mother's table without a word of explanation, letting her taste it and decide for herself.

"Pour it on," he said. "But not till the last second."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A down payment is the part of a home's price the buyer pays upfront so less must be borrowed; in British usage it is called a deposit.
story:
The notice had been taped to the building's front door for two days before Brittany texted Elliot a photo of it with the words ask your dad?? and three question marks. By Saturday afternoon he was on her floor with his laptop, a bag of chips between them, the notice itself flattened on the coffee table where her mother had left it. The landlord was selling the building. All tenants had ninety days.

"There has to be something we can do," Brittany said. "Like, legally."

Elliot read the notice again. He had assumed, in a vague way he was now embarrassed by, that rent was rent, that you paid it and the apartment stayed yours the way a backpack stayed yours. The notice used words he only half knew. He typed them into the search bar one at a time.

"Okay, so when we moved here my mom paid first month, last month, and a security deposit," Brittany said, reading over his shoulder. "That's like five thousand dollars she doesn't have again. If we have to move, that money comes back, but the new place wants it before the old place gives it back. It's a trap." She said the last word with real feeling, and Elliot didn't argue, though "trap" implied someone had designed it, some landlord's machination, when it seemed more like a machine nobody had built on purpose.

He went home and asked his father, who was circumspect in the way he always was about money, answering some questions and sliding past others. They had rented until Elliot was nine. Then, in the year the interest rates dipped, his parents had bought. Elliot remembered the summer as a summer of boxes and his father's bad mood. What he hadn't known, until his father pulled a folder from the filing cabinet, was that they had handed over most of their savings first, tens of thousands of dollars, before the bank would lend them the rest.

"Nobody just gives you a mortgage," his father said. "You have to put skin in."

On Monday, Elliot stopped at the bank on Delancey to ask about it, mostly so he could tell Brittany something concrete. The adviser at the desk was Ms. Njoroge, who had coached his little brother's soccer team two springs ago and still greeted him by name. He explained, awkwardly, that his friend's building was being sold and his parents had bought once and he was trying to understand how it all worked, and she pulled a brochure toward her and started sketching numbers on the back.

"Say the place is three hundred thousand," she said. "The buyer pays part of that price upfront, out of pocket. Then the loan covers the rest." She circled the smaller number. "That upfront part is the down payment."

"Like a deposit?" Elliot asked. "Brittany's mom paid a deposit on their apartment."

Ms. Njoroge smiled. "Same idea, different thing. In British usage, the down payment is called the deposit."

Elliot sat with that a moment. The same word doing two jobs, one that came back to you when you moved out, one that vanished into the price of the thing you were buying, so you had to borrow less. He thought of his father's bad mood that summer, the skin in.

"So when the landlord sells the building," he said slowly, "whoever buys it, they pay some upfront and borrow the rest, and then the rent we pay is partly going to their loan."

"That's one way a landlord's numbers can work," she said, and folded the brochure in half. "There are others."

He walked back to Brittany's with the paper she'd given him, and on the way he tried to codify what he'd learned into something he could actually say to her: that their rent, her mother's deposit, the buyer's down payment, the bank's mortgage were all pieces of one system, that the building being sold didn't mean they were being thrown away so much as passed along the chain. It sounded better in his head than it was going to sound out loud.

Brittany was on the fire escape smoking, which she did only when things were bad. He told her about the ninety days, about the security deposit trap she'd already mapped, and then, carefully, about the down payment, the upfront part of the price, the loan for the rest. She listened with her chin on her knees.

"So whoever buys this building," she said, "has to hand over a pile of cash first. Like my mom's deposit but a hundred times bigger, and they don't get it back."

"Basically," Elliot said. "And in England they literally call it the deposit. Same word."

She was quiet, ash lengthening on her cigarette. He had come ready to argue that the system wasn't a conspiracy, just arithmetic, and he realized he half believed it and half didn't, and that both halves could be true at once, the machine and the mood. He had changed his mind about something on the walk over, though he couldn't have said exactly what.

"Mom found a place on Halsey," Brittany said finally. "First, last, and deposit. She's asking my grandmother." She flicked the ash over the rail. "You want to help carry boxes Saturday?"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The basement of her grandfather's house smelled like furnace dust and the seven-layer dip Shayna's mother had sent along. Paige had the good chair, the one with the lever, because she had arrived first, which Shayna claimed was a scheme and Paige claimed was a competence. On the television, the university team was down by four with two minutes left, and Paige's grandfather kept saying "now watch this, now watch this," as though he had arranged the plays himself.

"Sit down," Shayna told Sage, who was pacing between the couch and the snack table. "You're making the receivers nervous."

"I'm making myself nervous," Sage said. "There's a difference. They get paid millions to be calm. I get chips."

Paige's grandfather muttered that nobody on that field would see a million dollars if football were run like the technocracy it was becoming, with analysts in booths deciding everything by spreadsheet, and her mother told him to hush, and he did not hush, but he lowered his volume to a level only the good chair could hear.

The quarterback rolled out. Paige had watched this team all season without caring much, and she had noticed something in herself, which was that on the plays that worked she thought "yes, we did it" and on the interceptions she thought "they threw that," and the switch happened without her permission, like a reflex in the knee. She had learned why in psychology in the spring, a study from 1976 by a man named Robert Cialdini, and the study had stuck with her more than the midterm it was tested on. He found that students wore more of their university's clothing after the football team won, and that when they described a win they said "we," and when they described a loss they didn't. She had written it down in the margin of her notebook and then drawn a small crown next to it for reasons she no longer remembered.

The pass was caught. A field goal went through as time expired, and the basement detonated. Her grandfather stood up so fast the footrest banged shut. Sage did a lap around the pool table with both arms up, knocked over the bowl of chips, and did not stop.

"We won," Sage shouted. "We won, we won, we won."

"You're wearing a jersey from a different university," Paige said.

"It's my dad's, it was clean, and we won."

"You've never played a down in your life."

"Neither have you, and you cried at halftime."

"That was onions," Paige said, which was a lie, and everyone knew it was a lie, and Shayna patted her knee in a way that absolved her of nothing.

Monday morning, Paige walked through the campus parking lot near her house, the one students used for the commuter lot, and counted. She counted on Tuesday too, because Monday after a win could be anything, a fluke, a hangover, a sale at the bookstore. After the win, she counted fourteen university sweatshirts, three hats, and one pugnacious old man in a car with the mascot on the license plate who honked at her for crossing too slowly. On Tuesday she counted eleven. The following autumn, after a loss, she counted four, and one of those was a kid who looked like he had slept in the sweatshirt rather than chosen it.

"You're doing your weird clipboard thing again," Shayna said, finding her at lunch.

"It's not weird, it's a study. 1976. Cialdini. People wear more school stuff after a win."

"That's the guy from the class where you drew the crown."

"The crown was decorative," Paige said. "And there's more. People say 'we' when the team wins and not when it loses. Watch Sage sometime. He's been saying 'we' since Saturday. When they lose in November, he'll say 'they couldn't run the ball.'"

"That's sad."

"It's not sad. It's just what happens." She turned her clipboard over, though she had nothing to hide. "The part I haven't figured out is whether it's a bad thing. Basking in it. If you take credit you didn't earn, that seems like a lie, but if it makes people feel like part of something, maybe it's not. I did it Saturday. I said 'we' in my own head and I didn't even notice until after."

Shayna stole one of her fries. "So what's your considered position, professor?"

"I don't have one yet. Both things are true and I can't make them cancel out."

Sage arrived at the table in a university hoodie, sleeves pushed up, tag still on. "What are we arguing about?"

"Whether you're a liar," Shayna said.

"Only on weekends," Sage said, and pulled the tag off with his teeth.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Most of Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights, published in 1847, is told by the housekeeper Nelly Dean to the visitor Lockwood, so events reach readers through two narrators with their own biases.
story:
Logan arrived at the book club with the novel held shut by a rubber band, because the spine had given up sometime around chapter nine. Nine people sat in a circle of folding chairs in the corner of the library that smelled faintly of the janitor's floor wax, and Ms. Henry was pouring apple juice from a dented thermos as though it were a sacrament. He had read the whole book, which he considered a personal triumph, and he had a page of notes in his back pocket, which he considered evidence of a life going wrong.

The trouble was that he had read it as a story about a house and some weather and people shouting across a moor, and everyone else seemed to have read some other, sharper book. Rosie opened the discussion by saying she hated Heathcliff, and Joelle said that was the point, and Rosie said no, the point was that she still liked him anyway, and the two of them conducted this argument like it was a sport they'd trained for.

Then Joelle leaned forward and asked a question that stopped the circle cold. "Do we actually know Heathcliff? Most of the book is Nelly telling it. The housekeeper. She tells it all to Lockwood, the visitor who rents the place, and he writes it down. Do we ever get anybody straight, or just Nelly's version?"

Logan felt the page of notes in his pocket become heavier, or possibly irrelevant. He had noticed Nelly. He had noticed she was always in the room, tidying something, interrupting at the worst moments. He had assumed she was furniture. Now she was rearranging the entire building.

"She doesn't like Catherine," Rosie said. "You can hear it. She calls her proud and wild, but she says it like she's enjoying herself."

"She watched everything," Joelle said. "Twenty years of it. And she's the only tap. Everything we know comes through her, then through him, and then to us. Two narrators, both with their hands on the story."

Logan raised his hand, then felt ridiculous, since no one else was raising theirs, and lowered it while keeping the question. "So when she says Heathcliff is a devil, is that a fact or an opinion?"

"It's a report," Joelle said. "The question is whether reports from her are worth anything."

Ms. Henry refilled her cup and said nothing, which Logan was beginning to understand was her coaching style. She had the phlegmatic patience of someone who had watched forty years of teenagers discover things she'd known all along, and she treated these detonations like weather, worth noting, not worth preventing.

Logan got home and read the frame chapters again, the ones he'd skimmed because Lockwood seemed like a buffoon, which he was, dreaming of a ghost and forcing Nelly to sit with him through a illness he'd mostly invented. But the buffoon was the filter. Everything in the middle of the book, published in 1847 and standing there in Logan's rubber-banded copy, reached him because a housekeeper had decided to tell it, and a visitor had decided to write it down, and neither of them was Emily Brontë, and neither of them was neutral. He made a diagram on the back of his history notes: moor, house, Nelly, Lockwood, reader, with arrows going one direction only. It looked like a plumbing schematic. He found this both funny and faintly disturbing, like learning his own eyes had been installed by a contractor with opinions.

At the next meeting, he brought the diagram. Rosie laughed at the arrows. Joelle turned it upside down, considered it, and turned it back. "Okay," she said. "But here's the thing that keeps me up. Nelly's a virtuoso at this. She's not lying exactly. She's choosing. Every scene she's in, she's the reasonable one, the one who warned everybody. She's editing herself into the moral center of a story where she keeps making things worse."

"So we can't trust her," Rosie said.

"We can't not trust her," Joelle said. "She's all we have."

Logan looked at his diagram and tried to titrate the two positions, adding a little of Joelle's suspicion to his original certainty that the story simply happened, watching the color change without being sure what the final mixture proved. "I think it's both," he said slowly. "She's biased, and she's the only witness. I trust her about what happened. I don't trust her about what it meant. The meaning's the part where she gets to choose, so that's the part I have to do myself." He heard how much he was claiming for himself and added, "Probably badly."

Rosie said that was the most responsible thing anyone had said in that library all year, possibly including the librarian. Ms. Henry wrote something on her clipboard, which she never showed anyone, and Logan suspected it was a grocery list, and suspected equally that it was not.

He still didn't know whether Heathcliff loved Catherine or only loved winning her, and he said so, out loud, and nobody rescued him from it. Joelle refilled his cup from the dented thermos without being asked.

"Next month," Rosie announced, tapping the cover of the new book. "First-person narrator. Supposedly very reliable."

"Auditioning," Logan said, "for a book club."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
The community center rented its practice rooms for four dollars an hour, cash only, and Sienna had learned to bring exact change because the woman at the front desk never opened the register after six. Room 3 smelled like floor polish and the ghost of somebody's curry from the microwave down the hall. She had chosen the cello because her grandmother had left one in the attic, and because Sydney had said, on the first day of senior year, that if Sienna didn't find one thing to do that wasn't for college applications she was going to turn into a spreadsheet. Sienna had laughed and then not laughed, because it felt true.

The problem was that after three months she still sounded like she was interrogating the instrument. Her left hand pressed the strings hard enough to leave grooves in her fingertips, and the notes came out either flat or sharp, mostly sharp, and she couldn't tell which by ear yet. So she'd spent eleven dollars of her tutoring money on a clip-on tuner, a little plastic eye that stared at the A string and judged her.

That was where the number showed up. She was plucking the A, open string, no fingers, and the tuner read 440. Fine. Then she tried the same note higher, the A her teacher had marked with a penciled circle on the fingerboard chart, and the little screen said 880. Sienna stared at it, plucked again, watched the needle settle. Exactly double. She checked the string was still in tune, then played the high A again, then the low one, back and forth like she was testing whether the machine was lying to her.

"You're going to wear out that string," said Kayla from the doorway. Kayla had a key to the building because her mother ran the Tuesday night bingo, and she had taken to doing her chemistry homework in Room 4 to escape the noise of the callers. "Also you made that face for like five minutes."

"It doubled," Sienna said. "The number. A is 440, and the A above it is 880. Exactly twice. That can't be a coincidence."

Kayla came in and sat on the folded chairs stacked against the wall. "Sounds like the kind of thing that's either a coincidence or math."

"Same note, one octave up, and it vibrates at twice the frequency." Sienna turned the tuner so Kayla could see. "I'm not making it up, it's right there."

Kayla squinted at the screen, which offered no argument. "Huh. Eighty-eight's my grandma's lucky number, so honestly this feels auspicious." She went back to her homework, and Sienna went back to the A string, but something had rearranged itself in her head. The octave had always been a mystery, a thing you were supposed to feel, and it turned out it was also arithmetic. The same note lived at two addresses, one exactly twice the other, and knowing that didn't make her fingers any more accurate, but it made the whole project feel less like weather and more like a map.

She had promised her parents she would practice forty minutes a day, a promise they'd extracted as recompense for the drive across town twice a week, and most days she honored it. But there was a Wednesday in November when she didn't, because Sydney's brother had gone to the hospital overnight, nothing fatal, a cracked wrist from a skateboard, but Sydney had texted and then gone silent in a way that meant she was alone with it. Sienna absconded from Room 3 with the cello still in its case and went to Sydney's house with two teas from the place by the bus stop, and they sat on the porch steps while the tea went cold, and that was the practice she did instead.

The next week a note was taped to Room 3's door in Ms. Leung's small square handwriting. Ms. Leung taught the Wednesday morning seniors' choir in the big hall and had caught Sienna practicing early more than once. The note said: To the cellist. My singers keep asking who is making that sound in the afternoons. I told them a girl who is getting better, which they did not entirely believe in October but believe now. Come find me if you ever want to play for people who will clap at anything. We are a forgiving audience and we bring snacks. Room 5, Wednesdays at ten. Sienna read it twice, then folded it into the pocket of her cello case, where it made a small rectangle she could feel through the fabric for the rest of the afternoon.

She thought about the two ways of understanding the octave, because she could not stop thinking about it, plucking her open A and watching the tuner and then reaching for the 880 and watching it again. There was the fact, clean and doubled, and there was the sound, which no number had ever contained, the way the two notes fit inside each other like a cupped hand. She suspected she would spend years learning what the arithmetic couldn't tell her, and she was honest enough with herself to admit she didn't yet know how the two things added up, only that both were true at once.

On the following Wednesday she cut her chemistry study hall, which Kayla covered for by submitting Sienna's lab data with a specious excuse about a dentist appointment, and wheeled the cello down the corridor to Room 5. The choir was twelve people with an average age of about seventy, and they did clap at anything, and one woman in a purple cardigan brought date squares. Sienna played her A, then the A above it, and Ms. Leung leaned toward the singers and said, "Hear that? Same note, twice as fast," and Sienna, blushing, said, "Twice the frequency," and the woman in the purple cardigan said, "Play it again, dear, the double one," and she did.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Paul Boyer and John Walker shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP.
story:
The overhead fan in the science lab moved the smell of ammonia around without clearing it, and Layla copied the diagram from the board a third time: glucose, then the long corridor of arrows, then the mitochondrion with its folded inner wall, and finally the small bright letters, ATP. She could reproduce every step on paper. What she could not do was say why the sequence mattered, and the unit test on Monday would ask for both.

Amaya wanted the diagram finished by four o'clock, because she had a shift at the garden centre and no patience for mysteries. Joe sat across the bench with his laptop open, supposedly fact-checking their labels, though Layla had noticed he kept drifting toward basketball scores. Ms. Bakker moved between the benches, correcting the recalcitrant Bunsen burner on the far table, saying nothing to them yet, which meant either that their work was fine or that she was waiting for them to find the flaw themselves.

"Here's what I don't get," Layla said. "The last arrow. Oxygen goes in, ATP comes out. That's the part everyone just writes down." She tapped the page. "Ms. Bakker keeps saying we should be able to trace it, not just recite it. There has to be something between the oxygen and the ATP."

Amaya checked the clock. "It's an enzyme thing. There's always an enzyme thing. Write 'enzyme-mediated' and let's go."

Joe turned his laptop around without a word. He had actually been researching, Layla saw, and not scores; the screen showed a page about ATP synthase, the enzyme that built the ATP itself, sitting in the inner membrane like a turbine in a dam. He shrugged when she looked at him. "I got curious. You kept asking why."

"You could have said something an hour ago."

"You were busy being certain it was unknowable."

Ms. Bakker arrived behind them quietly, the way she did, and read the screen over Layla's shoulder. She did not explain it. She only said, "Follow that thread. Find out what it cost to work out." Then she moved on, and Layla understood that this was the assignment now, the real one, disguised as a suggestion.

She took the laptop and read. The account was plainer than she expected: Paul Boyer and John Walker had shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP. Layla read the sentence twice. A Nobel Prize, for one enzyme, for the explanation of a single step in the diagram she had been copying as though it were household information. Someone had spent decades on that arrow. Amaya leaned over, restless, and Layla said the sentence aloud to her, partly to fix it in her own memory. "Boyer and Walker shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for explaining how ATP synthase makes ATP." Amaya wrote it in the margin, in her fast slanted hand, and said, "Fine, it's famous, can we glue the model together now?"

Layla sat with the strange doubling of it for a moment. Her own habit was to treat knowledge as inventory, facts to be collected and deployed, the way Amaya treated time, as something to be budgeted and never squandered. But Joe had shown her the other way, following a question because it was there, letting curiosity expropriate an afternoon that was supposed to belong to a checklist. She had always thought of those approaches as rivals, the efficient and the wandering, and now she suspected they were complicity more than competition, that you needed the discipline of the diagram and the stubbornness of the question, and that the test on Monday might reward whichever one she fed. Or both. She could not yet say which, and she decided she was allowed not to know that.

She did know one thing: her poster was going to have the enzyme on it, drawn large, with the two names underneath. She pulled the poster board toward her and began sketching the mitochondrion's folded wall, this time from the inside, where the work happened. Amaya cut out the paper arrows without complaining again, because the four o'clock deadline had quietly become four thirty, and Joe slid the laptop back to the middle of the bench where all three of them could see it.

Ms. Bakker passed their table one last time before the bell. She looked at the half-finished sketch, at the sentence in the margin, and at the three of them leaning over the same bench. She picked up the marker, and beneath Layla's drawing of the enzyme she wrote a single word: trace. Layla capped the marker for her and started at the top of the poster, at glucose, and drew the first arrow of the long road down.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: The term 'unreliable narrator' was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction.
story:
Hudson had read the novel twice before the essay was due, which was one more time than strictly necessary, and both times he had believed the narrator completely, which turned out to be the problem.

Ms. Shin handed the drafts back on a Tuesday, third period, and walked the rows without commenting until she reached his desk. "You've written 'the narrator is obviously lying about the fire,'" she said, tapping the page. "'Obviously' is doing a lot of work there. Where did you get the phrase 'unreliable narrator,' by the way?"

"I don't know," Hudson said. "It's just the word for it."

"It is a word for it. Find out where it came from and tell us Thursday." She moved on, and he sat there feeling like he'd been caught borrowing something without asking.

At lunch he spread the draft out on the table in the corner of the cafeteria where he and Kai always sat, near the window so Kai could see the parking lot, which mattered to him for reasons he'd never explained and Hudson had never asked. "She wants me to trace a phrase," he said. "Like it's a bug."

"Maybe it is a bug," Kai said, peeling an orange and pushing half of it across the table without looking, the way he did when he guessed Hudson had skipped breakfast. "You use words all day that other people made up and you never wonder who."

Hudson ate the orange. That afternoon in the library he found a shelf of criticism behind the study carrels, dusty in a way that suggested nobody his age had been there recently, and pulled down a thick book called The Rhetoric of Fiction. The critic's name was Wayne C. Booth. The book had come out in 1961, more than sixty years before Hudson was born, and Booth had coined the term there, in pages dense enough that he had to read the same paragraph three times. He wrote the details on his hand because his notebook was in his locker, and the ink smeared against his jeans by the time he got home.

What stayed with him, though, wasn't the citation. It was a distinction Booth drew that Hudson couldn't stop chewing on: a narrator could be unreliable without being a liar, could be sincere and wrong, could withhold out of shame rather than deceit. He went back to the novel that night with two highlighters, one colour for things the narrator said that other characters contradicted, and one for things he simply declined to say. The second colour turned out to mark more of the book, which unsettled him, because absence was harder to argue about than falsehood. You could call someone a liar. You couldn't easily call them a gap.

On Thursday, Ms. Shin let the discussion run to him. "So," she said. "The term. Who made it up?"

"The critic Wayne C. Booth," Hudson said. "In his book The Rhetoric of Fiction, in 1961. He coined it."

"And does knowing that change your essay?"

He hadn't expected the question and stalled for a second, and from two rows over Ian, who usually slept through this class, said, "Tell him about the highlighters," which was strange, since Hudson hadn't told Ian about the highlighters. Ian shrugged. "You were talking to yourself at your locker yesterday. Loudly."

Hudson laughed, and the laughing made the next part easier. He explained the two colours, the lies versus the omissions, and said that his original draft had treated the narrator's account as noxious, an act of pure bad faith, when it might be closer to an act of self-protection. "He's not fabricating the fire," Hudson said. "He's interpolating. He fills in the parts he can't remember with what he needs to be true, and he doesn't know he's doing it, which means the reader has to do the knowing for him."

"So can we trust him or not?" Ms. Shin asked.

"That's what I can't decide," Hudson said, and heard a couple of people exhale the way people do when someone refuses to land the plane. "Trust isn't binary. Booth's whole point is that the author sets up a relationship between the narrator and the reader, and the narrator broke it, but the author didn't, so maybe the artifice is the honest part. The book tells you the truth by teaching you to doubt it. But I don't know where the line is between a narrator who's hiding and a narrator who's blind. I don't think Booth fully draws it either."

After class, Kai caught him in the hallway and fell into step. "You sounded like you actually read that giant book."

"I read about nine pages of it."

"Still counts." They passed the trophy case, and Kai slowed down, glancing at the glass. "That thing you said, about filling in what you can't remember with what you need to be true. Do people do that? Not narrators. People."

Hudson thought of his own essay, the confident "obviously," and of how quickly he'd written it, and how the smeared ink on his hand had washed off by dinner as though the source had never mattered. "Probably," he said. "It's harder to catch in yourself, though. You'd need the second highlighter colour for your own head."

Kai was quiet until they reached the doors. "Then lend me a highlighter," he said. "I've got something to show you after practice."

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: At 7 percent annual growth compounded yearly, $1,000 grows to almost $15,000 in forty years, so money saved at eighteen can multiply many times by retirement.
story:
Addison had folded the campus map into a square small enough to hold in one hand, and she kept unfolding a corner of it outside the finance building, where a table of orange juice and pamphlets had been set out for the open house. Her paycheck from the bookstore was direct-deposited on Fridays, one hundred and eighty-two dollars, and she had been carrying the number around all morning like a stone in her pocket. Jerry was already inside, waving at her from the second row of a lecture hall where a student panel was answering questions.

"I'm going to ask about the dorms," Jerry whispered when she sat down. "You should ask about scholarships."

She didn't ask about scholarships. On the panel, a senior with a lanyard full of pins was saying that the biggest mistake first-years made was treating money as something to think about later, and Addison wrote down only that sentence, pressing hard enough that it showed through the page. Afterward the crowd drifted toward the free food, but she stayed in her seat doing arithmetic on the back of the map. Seven percent a year, her mother had said once, was a reasonable thing to hope for; whatever that meant. She doubled one thousand dollars, then doubled it again, and kept going until the numbers stopped meaning anything.

"You look like you're doing taxes," said Alia, dropping into the seat beside her. Alia was in her homeroom and had somehow talked the guidance office into letting her come on the trip even though she was a junior.

"Seven percent," Addison said. "If it's compounded yearly." She turned the map so Alia could see. "One thousand dollars grows to almost fifteen thousand dollars in forty years."

Alia squinted at it. "Forty years. We'll be fifty-eight."

"So money saved at eighteen can multiply many times by the time we retire. Like, I save a thousand now and it turns into fifteen thousand without me doing anything." She heard how it sounded and felt embarrassed anyway. "I mean, not without anything. Time does it."

"My mom would impute that to luck," Alia said. "If someone ended up with fifteen grand, she'd say they got lucky, not that they waited." She said it lightly, but there was a line underneath it, something about the people Alia's mother worked with at the hospital, people who had never had a spare thousand dollars at any age. Addison wanted to ask and didn't.

Mr. Fischer, who had driven the van and was standing at the back of the hall with his coffee, caught her eye as they filed out. "Find something interesting in there?"

"A number," she said. "A thousand turning into almost fifteen thousand."

He nodded, said nothing, and held the door. She was grateful for that, and also slightly annoyed, because she had half wanted him to tell her whether it was true.

The afternoon dissolved into tours. Jerry dragged them through the recreation centre and then the dining hall, where he sampled everything offered and Alia kept a running commentary on the detractors of campus food, the people who complained online, versus the reality of the pasta, which was decent. But in the student centre, on a wall of bulletin boards, Addison found a flyer for a first-year personal finance seminar, and beside it a corkboard where students had pinned index cards of advice. One card, in green ink, said only: started at nineteen, thank you, past self.

She stood in front of it long enough that Alia came back for her.

"Okay," Alia said. "You've been weird since the lecture. What is it?"

"My paycheck," Addison said. "It's a hundred and eighty-two dollars. And my phone bill is forty, and I owe my mom for the shoes, and there's the deposit I keep not making. But if I saved even a hundred a month from now, by forty years it's not a hundred a month anymore. It's all of it, multiplied." She heard herself rushing, the inchoate version of a plan she hadn't finished thinking, and slowed down. "That's the argument for waiting on the shoes. That's the argument for a lot of things."

"And the argument against?"

Addison looked at the index card. Past self. The person she was supposed to be thanking at fifty-eight didn't exist yet, and the person she was now wanted the shoes and owed her mother and had a college fund shaped like a hole. She could hold both ideas; that was the strange part. Saving felt like faith in a version of herself she couldn't picture, and spending felt like loyalty to the one she actually was.

"I don't know yet," she said. "I know the math. I don't know what I owe to which me."

Alia pulled a pen from her bag, tore a page from her notebook, and wrote something against the corkboard's edge, then pinned the paper beside the green-ink card. "For next year's version of us," she said.

Addison leaned over to read it. The page said: still deciding, come back later.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Ramadan, many Muslims break each day's fast at the sunset meal, iftar, by first eating a date, following the practice of the Prophet Muhammad.
story:
Sophia's grandmother had led the iftar for forty years, and this year, without ceremony, she had handed it over. "You," she said in April, pressing the battered ring binder into Sophia's hands as though bestowing a sceptre. "I get tired standing. You don't." The binder held everything: the prayer timetable for the city, the shopping lists, the note in her grandmother's careful script about how many dates to set out, who took tea and who took only water, which cousin was allergic to lentils. Sophia had read it three times on the bus out to the house, which sat near the river, its windows opening onto the riparian tangle of willows and reeds that turned gold in the late afternoon.

The trouble began with the numbers. The timetable folded inside the binder, printed years ago, gave sunset as 7:39. Sophia's phone, which located her precisely at her grandmother's kitchen table, insisted on 7:42. Three minutes. It seemed like nothing until she understood that everything depended on the moment: the dates had to be ready at the second the fast broke, not a minute before, not a minute after, because her grandmother did not like to wait once the sun was down, and neither, it turned out, did anyone else.

She called Nikita, who was not Muslim but who had fasted in solidarity for a week last year and gave up halfway through lunch on day three. "Three minutes is nothing," Nikita said. "Just split the difference." "You can't split the difference with the sun," Sophia said. She explained what she'd learned from the binder's first page, where her grandmother had written it out plainly so no one in the family could claim ignorance: the sunset meal was called iftar, and it began, always, with a date, because that was how the Prophet Muhammad had broken his fast. "A date," Nikita repeated. "Like the fruit." "Like the fruit." Sophia could hear her own voice doing that thing it did when she was nervous, going flat and certain at the same time.

Her grandmother, she realized, wanted something more particular than three minutes of accuracy. All afternoon the old woman moved through the kitchen in her slow way, straightening what was already straight, and Sophia began to see that what her grandmother wanted was to be replaced by someone who understood that the dates were not a snack. They were the hinge of the whole evening, the first thing to touch a tongue that had tasted nothing since dawn. Sophia washed the medjools and slit each one open with a paring knife, checking for the possibility of a pit, arranging them on the blue dish that came out only for this. She set the dish on the table where the last light would reach it.

At 7:30 she could not find the prayer beads. Her grandmother always held them through the final stretch of the afternoon, turning them while the light thinned, and their absence made the house feel improperly arranged, like a word missing from a sentence. Sophia searched the sitting room, the windowsill, the drawer of the sideboard that smelled of camphor. She found them at last hooked over the tap in the bathroom, which was so unlike her grandmother that Sophia stood holding them, uncertain whether she had discovered a small collapse or simply an aging woman's forgettable afternoon.

She brought the beads to her grandmother, who took them without comment, but whose fingers closed around them with a virtuoso's ease, each bead finding its place in sequence without her looking down. The sun lowered itself into the willows along the river. In the kitchen the samosas were keeping warm, the lentils were thickening, and Sophia stood between the old timetable and her phone and chose. She chose the paper, because it was her grandmother's, and because if she was wrong she would rather be wrong in her grandmother's way.

At 7:38 she put the dish of dates in the middle of the table. The family gathered, her parents and the aunties and the small cousins who had not fasted but had been made to feel the weight of the day anyway. Nobody spoke. Sophia watched the window, the sky gone the colour of a bruised peach, and when the paper's minute arrived she lifted the dish and offered it first to her grandmother, because that was also written in the binder, the order of it, the eldest first. Her grandmother took a date and ate it slowly, and the room exhaled, and everyone reached at once.

Whether the sun had truly set at 7:39 or 7:42, Sophia would never know. Nobody checked. Her grandmother turned another bead and looked out at the darkening river and said, "Tomorrow, check the dates earlier. The small ones stick to the dish."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or number.
story:
The article was in Korean, fourteen lines of it, printed from Samy's mother's laptop, and it concerned a festival in a coastal town whose name Chase could not yet pronounce. His task, supposedly simple, was to read it aloud and then say in his own words what it was about. Samy's family had moved here two years ago, and Samy had offered to tutor him because Chase had signed up for the exchange trip in spring and could currently introduce himself, count to twenty, and confess, in the new language, that he did not understand anything, which was at least a true sentence.

"Start here," Samy said, sliding the page across the kitchen table. Katherine had claimed the chair by the window and was theoretically doing her own homework, though her actual occupation seemed to be eating Samy's crackers and offering commentary.

Chase read the first line, character by character, sounding out each syllable the way he had in kindergarten. A minute later he was still on the second line. "There's a date in here somewhere," he said. "The festival has to be on a date. I'm looking for the date."

"Then stop reading it," Katherine said, crumbs visible on her sleeve, which undermined her authority somewhat.

"I can't stop reading it, I'm reading it."

Samy leaned over and spun the paper so it faced him. "You're doing two different jobs at once. Skimming means reading quickly for the general idea, while scanning means searching a text for one specific detail such as a name or a number. You want the date? That's scanning. Don't read. Hunt." He ran a finger down the page fast, not stopping anywhere, then tapped a cluster of characters near the end. "Numbers look like this. There, and there."

Chase felt the small humiliation of a thing that had been obvious to everyone but him. He had spent four minutes decoding adjectives about the sea when he had needed one number. "So I scan for the date first," he said slowly, "and then I skim the rest for the gist, and I only actually read the parts that matter."

"Look at him," Katherine said to Samy. "One fact and he thinks he's perspicacious."

"I didn't say perspicacious."

"You were thinking it loudly." She pointed a cracker at him. "Also you owe me, because I quizzed you on biology terms for an hour last week while you prevaricated about whether you'd studied. You had not."

That was fair, Chase conceded, though he did not concede it aloud. What he did instead was run his eyes down the article the way Samy had, fast and shallow, letting the characters that repeated themselves catch at his attention like burrs. Two of them appeared over and over, and when he hunted down their meanings in the vocabulary list Samy had made, they turned out to be the town's name and the word for festival. So the article was about a festival in a town. It had a date, which he had scanned and found, and there was a paragraph near the middle about lanterns, which he could tell because a character Samy had taught him early, the one for light, kept surfacing there like a fish rising.

"There are lanterns," Chase announced. "And a parade, maybe, there's a word that keeps showing up that might be parade or might be procession or might be a type of soup, I honestly can't tell you which."

"It's parade," Samy said. "Good enough. Now say the whole summary."

Chase sat up, aware of Katherine watching, aware of his own voice being about to do something embarrassing in a language he did not own. He gave it three sentences: a festival, in a coastal town, on a date in autumn, with lanterns and a parade, and an emphasis in the last paragraph he couldn't quite name, something about the town welcoming visitors. His pronunciation of the town's name came out wrong twice and almost right the third time. Samy said, "Again," and Chase said the name again, and this time it landed, the syllables clicking into each other like parts of something fitted together.

"See, this is mutualism," Katherine said, gesturing with the last cracker at the two of them. "You learn Korean, Samy gets somebody to practice explaining English with, and I get crackers and entertainment. Everyone profits."

"Those are Samy's crackers," Chase pointed out.

"Then it's mutualism between me and Samy, and you're the landscape."

Samy printed a second article, shorter, about a market, and set it on the table between them. "Same drill," he said. "But this time you scan for the hours first. Find me the numbers." Chase picked up the page, and before reading anything at all, he let his eyes drop straight down the column, hunting.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: Informed consent in medicine means a patient agrees to treatment after being told its risks, benefits and alternatives in words they can understand.
story:
The automatic doors exhaled a gust of air-conditioning that smelled of carpet cleaner and coffee, and William stepped into the bank holding his birth certificate, his passport, forty dollars in a zippered bag, and a plan he had rehearsed on the bus. He wanted a savings account. Not a card with a logo, not an app with a cartoon coin, an account, because the car he was rebuilding with Terence needed a cylinder head, and the cylinder head cost three hundred and twenty dollars, and his mother could not give him that, and he had decided he was done deciding that for her.

"Take a ticket," said the machine. It spat out a slip reading B-47, and beneath it, in small grey print, terms subject to change without notice. He read the print twice. It seemed to be warning him about the very ticket in his hand.

Antonia had come with him because she had opened her own account the month before and because, she said, she liked watching him attempt anything official. She sat with her boots on the rung of the chair, unwrapping a mint. "You're going to read the whole pamphlet," she said. "I can feel it."

"I read your pamphlet last month. There was a part about liability."

"There's always a part about liability." She offered him a mint. He took it.

When B-47 lit up, they were shown to a desk belonging to Mr. Brown, who had reading glasses pushed up into white hair and a mug reading WORLD'S OKAYEST BOWLER. He laid out a form with the calm of a man laying a table. "This is the account agreement," he said. "You're sixteen, so a parent countersigns. Fees are on page two. If your balance drops below fifty, there's a maintenance charge." He turned the page himself, which William noted, and appreciated, and did not entirely trust.

"What's the charge if I overdraft?" William asked.

"Thirty-five dollars per occurrence."

William looked at the number. "So if I buy something for a dollar with four dollars in the account, I owe you thirty-six dollars."

"That's the term, yes."

"Is there an alternative? Like the account declining instead?"

Mr. Brown's glasses came down from his hair. "There is. Most young people don't ask."

Two weeks earlier, William had sat in a clinic waiting room with Antonia, who was seventeen and needed a physical before her swimming season. He had gone along because her mother was working and because Antonia claimed she got "pre-signature amnesia," a condition, she insisted, well documented in the physiology of her family. When the clipboard came, Antonia slid it toward the pen like it was radioactive. William picked it up first.

The form said consent to treatment and listed things in a font designed, he suspected, to be impermeable to teenagers. He read a line about a reaction to the tetanus vaccine and stopped. "What's this reaction?" he asked the nurse when she came in. "How likely, and how bad?"

She didn't sigh, which surprised him. "Sore arm, fever, one in a million something worse. The benefit is protection from tetanus, and the alternative is skipping it and taking that risk instead."

"In words I can understand," William said, "that's the whole idea, right? You tell me risks, benefits, alternatives, and then I agree."

"It's called informed consent," she said, and seemed pleased someone had asked.

"Then explain everything on this form that way," he said, "and she'll sign." Antonia signed. She flexed her arm afterward and said the soreness proved her theory about her family, and he laughed so hard a toddler in the waiting room laughed too, for no reason except that laughing is contagious, which is also physiology, probably.

In the bank, Mr. Brown was drawing a small diagram. "Decline instead of overdraft, we call that opt-in courtesy," he said. "You initial here, and here."

William read the paragraph the initials referred to. It used the word liability three times and the word cardholder twice, and once, spectacularly, the word indemnify, which he circled with his pen. "Indemnify," he said.

"You cover us if someone misuses the card."

"Define misuse."

From Antonia's angle, watching the two of them lean over the form like chess players, the whole thing looked like a duel conducted in felt-tip. She could see Mr. Brown enjoying it, in his quiet way; he kept refilling William's water cup from the cooler even though William had drunk none of it. She thought about the clinic, how William had held the clipboard like it was a contract trying to trick him, which, she supposed, it sort of was, and which was also why she had brought him here today instead of just telling him what to initial. He circumscribe-tested everything. That was not the word; she didn't have the word. But he walked the edges of things, checking where they ended.

"Page four," William said finally. "It says you can change the terms and notify me. Notify me how?"

"Letter to your address."

"And if I've moved?"

"Then you weren't notified," Mr. Brown said, "but you agreed anyway."

William sat back. That sentence was the whole afternoon in miniature, he thought: a deal where one side could change the deal. His mother signed things like that all the time, quickly, tired, at kitchen tables and car windows. Maybe there was nothing wrong with it and maybe there was something very wrong with it and he genuinely could not tell which, and he was not going to pretend he could. What he could do was read every word this once, and ask every question this once, and initial the box that stopped the thirty-five-dollar fee, and put his name down for the cylinder head.

He signed at the bottom, slowly, the way Antonia had signed at the clinic, and slid the form across. "Countersignature's for my mum. She'll read it too."

Mr. Brown took off his glasses. "Send her in," he said. "I'll put the kettle on."

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: In his 1975 book Discipline and Punish, Michel Foucault used Bentham's panopticon as a metaphor for how modern institutions control people through the possibility of constant observation.
story:
Jordan got to the coffee shop first and claimed the table by the window, where he could watch the register, the door and the pastry case all at once, which he did without meaning to. Old habit from senior year, when the school had installed monitoring software on every laptop and he had learned that someone, somewhere, might be watching the webcam light blink on. He spread his notes across the table: two pages for the debate he and Rayyan had to give in the fall seminar at the community college, on whether classroom monitoring software was a tool or a trap. The question had sounded simple in the catalogue. It was not simple now.

Rayyan arrived carrying a laptop with a sticker over its camera, which Jordan had always taken as a joke and now regarded as evidence. Rayyan wanted, more than anything, to win the debate, because winning meant the professor might recommend him for the ethics internship downtown, and Rayyan had said so twice already without shame.
